items.title: EVAL-5: make the eval reproduction runnable, and let Core CI be a required check
items.body:
`main` is green again — [#131](https://github.com/daemon-blockint-tech/4R3S/pull/131) did that. This is the part it did not cover, split out of the now-closed #132.

## 1. The documented reproduction never ran

`eval/predictions/README.md` documents how to regenerate `ares-latest.csv` — the only number that gates a release. Three defects, each fatal on its own:

| Step | Was | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `cargo build --release -p ares-cli` | `error: package ID specification 'ares-cli' did not match any packages`. The crate has three names — dir `crates/ares-cli/`, package `ares-v3`, binary `ares` — and `-p` takes the package |
| 4 | no `--fuzz false` | fuzzing defaults **on**; Trident init aborts on a staged dir (`Anchor.toml was not found in any parent directory`), so **all 159 scans fail** and step 5 converts an empty directory |
| 5 | `--reports` / `--manifest` | converter takes `--reports-dir` / `--staging-manifest`; argparse rejects these outright |

Fixed and re-run end to end. `--fuzz false` is also correct on principle, not just mechanically: this measures the deterministic static layer, and a fuzz campaign is not reproducible (GOLDEN RULE 2).

### What the run produces

| | |
|---|---|
| targets scanned | 159 (0 scan failures) |
| predictions | 220 rows |
| ground truth | 170 rows |
| precision | 0.7429 |
| recall | 0.4588 |
| **F1** | **0.5673** |

**The CSV this produced is byte-identical to the one #131 committed** — independent run, different checkout, different approach. Two independent reproductions agreeing is a far stronger determinism claim than either could make alone, and it is what makes the committed file *evidence* rather than one machine's snapshot. Recorded in the README so the next person does not have to re-establish it.

Stated just as plainly: this is **not** a publishable accuracy claim. Recall is under 0.5, and **ten of the fourteen** truth categories score 0.0000 because the static rule set emits nothing for them at all. `check_published_claims.py` still decides what may appear in a README, and it reads the CSV, not this table.

> A documented-but-unrunnable reproduction is the same as no reproduction. That is the whole point of GOLDEN RULE 3, and this was the reproduction for the release gate.

## 2. Core CI could not be a required check

Branch protection on `main` is now enabled. It **cannot** cover a path-filtered workflow: GitHub does not treat a required check that never runs as satisfied — it parks the PR on *"Expected — waiting for status to be reported"* indefinitely. The filter and the requirement are mutually exclusive.

The requirement is the half that matters: the incident was a grouped Dependabot cargo bump (`printpdf` 0.7 → 0.12.5) that failed Core CI and was merged anyway. So the `pull_request` path filter goes, and `Test` / `Lint and Format` / `Security Audit` become requireable.

`push` keeps its filter — nothing gates on push, so there is no deadlock to avoid and no reason to pay the minutes twice. Cost of the change: a Rust toolchain on TS-only PRs, running in parallel with everything else.

**After this merges**, these three should be added to the required set:

```bash
gh api -X PATCH repos/daemon-blockint-tech/4R3S/branches/main/protection/required_status_checks -f 'contexts[]=Test' -f 'contexts[]=Lint and Format' -f 'contexts[]=Security Audit'
```

Until then they are deliberately excluded, or every TS-only PR would hang.

## 3. A stale claim in `gate_selftest.py`

Its docstring said ARES *"has no committed prediction output yet, so CI cannot score the real system."* There is a committed CSV and CI does score it. Rewritten to say why the self-test still earns its keep: a threshold comparison that quietly stopped rejecting would wave any real score through, and inspecting the real score cannot reveal that.

## Not included, deliberately

#132 also set an F1 **regression floor** of 0.55. #131 made the opposite call — score without `--target-f1`, report the comparison informationally — with a clear rationale: blocking on a figure the README already disowns trains people to ignore a red check. That reasoning is sound and it is already merged, so this PR does not override it.

The gap it leaves is real though and worth deciding separately: with no floor at all, F1 could fall from 0.5673 to 0.20 and CI stays green. The informational report and a collapse-detecting floor are compatible.

## Verified

| | |
|---|---|
| `pytest eval` | 113 passed |
| `gate_selftest --target-f1 0.94` | green |
| `core-ci.yml` parses; declares all 3 jobs | ✅ |
| full 159-target regeneration | 0 scan failures, CSV matches `main` byte-for-byte |

items.title: docs: disclose the TRAIL precision boundary in the installed package (0.5.7)
items.body:
## Why

The README publishes TRAIL macro-F1 0.7535 and micro-F1 0.7463 as "reproducible from the
archive" and already discloses the in-distribution caveat (144 of 148 traces appeared in
calibration material). It omits the precision caveat that the sibling
[`pisama-detectors` README](https://github.com/Pisama-AI/pisama-detectors#archived-trail-platform-benchmark)
already carries. `pisama` is the package people actually install, and PyPI renders this
README, so the caveat needs to live here too.

## The fact, verified from the artifact

Parsed from `benchmarks/trail.json` in `Pisama-AI/pisama-detectors`:

| Check | Value |
|---|---|
| Categories with `fp = 0` | 14 of 14 |
| `prediction_count` | 813 |
| `mapped_annotations` | 813 |
| micro-recall (tp 481 / support 808) | 0.5953 |
| `2R / (1 + R)` | 0.7463 (equals the reported micro-F1 exactly) |
| macro-F1 recomputed from the 14 per-category F1 values | 0.7535 (equals the reported value) |

The archive scored only annotated errors, so no false positive was recordable. Precision is
1.000 by construction rather than by measurement, and F1 reduces to exactly `2R / (1 + R)`,
carrying no information beyond recall. `benchmarks/evidence.json` records the same boundary:
"The archive does not contain a negative candidate set that independently establishes
precision."

## What this PR does NOT claim

The F1 figures are not withdrawn or corrected. They are arithmetically reproducible from the
public confusion counts, exactly as the README says. The only addition is that they carry no
precision information, and that the informative figure is micro-recall 0.5953: the heuristic
tier alone missed roughly 40% of the labelled failures.

## Changes

- `README.md`: precision caveat added directly under the F1 line in **Benchmark Results**, plus
  a one-clause version in the intro paragraph (the part PyPI shows first).
- `pyproject.toml`, `src/pisama/__init__.py`: 0.5.6 to 0.5.7. A README fix only reaches users
  through a release, since PyPI renders the README from the published artifact.
- `CHANGELOG.md`: 0.5.7 entry, plus a backfilled 0.5.6 entry. The 0.5.6 release commit
  (f17a80f) bumped the version without a changelog entry, so the file jumped 0.5.5 to 0.5.7.
  The backfilled text is taken from that commit's own message and diff.

## Verification run locally (Python 3.13)

- `ruff check src tests` passed
- `mypy src/pisama` passed, no issues in 36 source files
- `pytest -q --cov=pisama --cov-fail-under=60` passed, 59 passed, coverage 61.73%
- `python -m build` plus `twine check dist/*` passed on both artifacts
- Confirmed the sdist `PKG-INFO` (what PyPI renders) carries the new caveat text and
  `Version: 0.5.7`; `pisama --version` reports 0.5.7

No source behavior changed. Docs, version, changelog only.

items.title: Add comic-text-detector and evaluation framework
items.body:
This PR introduces a trained text detector for comics and a framework to evaluate detection and recognition quality against hand-checked ground truth.

## Summary

The pipeline now supports two detection backends: the new `comic-text-detector` (trained on ~13k comic pages) and the existing CRAFT detector as a fallback. The comic detector provides text blocks with confidence scores and language detection in a single pass, eliminating the need for downstream geometry-based grouping. Additionally, a comprehensive evaluation module allows scoring runs against hand-corrected JSON to measure detection F1 and character error rate separately.

## Key Changes

**New Detection Backend:**
- Added `mangatrans/comicdetect.py`: Implements comic-text-detector using OpenCV's ONNX backend (no torch required)
  - `letterbox()`: Scales images to 1024² without stretching
  - `decode_blocks()`: Converts YOLO head output to boxes with NMS suppression
  - `columns_in()`: Extracts text columns/lines from the lettering mask
  - `ComicDetector`: Main detector class wrapping the ONNX model
- Added `mangatrans/detectors.py`: Unified detector interface
  - `Detection` and `DetectionResult` dataclasses for detector output
  - `model_path()`: Locates comic detector weights in cache or environment
  - `build()`: Factory function selecting detector based on availability
  - Support for `--detector auto|comic|craft` with fallback logic

**Evaluation Framework:**
- Added `mangatrans/evaluate.py`: Scoring module for ground truth comparison
  - `iou()`: Intersection-over-union for box matching
  - `edit_distance()`: Levenshtein distance for character error rate
  - `match()`: Greedy pairing of predicted and truth boxes
  - `Score` dataclass: Tracks detection metrics (precision, recall, F1) and recognition metrics (CER, exact match rate)
  - `score_page()` and `score_run()`: Compute scores for individual pages and entire runs
  - `report()`: Formatted output with per-page and aggregate statistics
  - `load_pages()`: Reads JSON from files or directories (supports both combined and per-page formats)

**Pipeline Integration:**
- Modified `mangatrans/pipeline.py`:
  - Added `keep_kinds()`: Determines which text types to keep based on detector capability
  - Extended `TextGroup` with `confidence`, `language`, and `drop_reason` fields
  - Added `dropped` list to `Page` to track filtered-out text with reasons
  - New `build_groups_from_blocks()`: Uses detector-provided blocks instead of geometry-based clustering
  - Updated `process_image()` to handle detector results with blocks and text masks
- Modified `mangatrans/detect.py`:
  - Wrapped CRAFT in `CraftDetector` class implementing common interface
  - Removed direct detector instantiation from pipeline

**CLI and Configuration:**
- Modified `mangatrans/cli.py`:
  - Added `--detector` argument with choices: `auto`, `comic`, `craft`
  - Updated `--text` argument to support `auto` mode (respects detector's grouping)
  - Added detector-specific thresholds: `--conf-threshold`, `--mask-threshold`
  - Added `eval` subcommand for scoring runs
- Modified `scripts/prefetch_models.py`:
  - Added `fetch_detector()` to download comic-text-detector weights from GitHub releases
  - Supports `--detector-only` flag to skip manga-ocr weights
  - Supports `--craft` flag to include CRAFT detector weights

**Testing:**
- Extended `test_grouping.py` with comprehensive detector and evaluation tests:
  - `_StubDetector`: Mock detector for testing block path without loading weights
  - Tests for letterbox padding, block decoding, NMS suppression
  - Tests for column/line extraction from lettering masks
  - Tests for block-to-group conversion and confidence handling
  - Tests for evaluation metrics (IOU, edit distance, scoring)

**Documentation:**
- Updated README with detector comparison table and workflow examples
- Updated module docstrings explaining detector choice and evaluation methodology
- Updated `manga_oc

items.title: Customer Churn Prediction — Random Forest Ensemble
items.body:
🌲 Customer Churn Prediction — Random Forest Ensemble

Predicting telecom customer churn with an ensemble of 100 decision trees — and a transparent audit of where the model wins, where it struggles, and what would fix it.

📌 Overview

Customer churn is one of the highest-leverage problems in telecom — every customer a model correctly flags as "at risk" is a retention offer that can be sent before it's too late, and every customer it misses is silent revenue loss. This project builds a Random Forest Classifier on the IBM Watson Telecom Customer Churn dataset and evaluates it the way a business stakeholder would: not just "what's the accuracy," but "which customers are we still losing, and why."

It's the ensemble-learning follow-up to an earlier single-tree churn model in this portfolio — same dataset, upgraded algorithm — and it's built specifically to compare two different ways of asking "which features matter": built-in Gini/entropy importance vs. Leave-One-Feature-Out (LOFO) impact testing.

📊 Dataset

Attribute | Detail -- | -- Source | IBM Watson Telecom Customer Churn dataset Records | 7,043 customers Raw Features | 20 (demographic, account, and service attributes) + target Target | Churn (Yes/No → binary encoded) Class Balance | ~26.5% churned / ~73.5% retained — moderately imbalanced

🚀 How to Run

git clone https://github.com/vishnusai2005/<repo-name>.git
cd <repo-name>
pip install -r requirements.txt
jupyter notebook "Random Forest Implementation.ipynb"

requirements.txt

├── assets/                              # Charts referenced in this README

🗺️ Roadmap

  • [ ] Hyperparameter tuning via GridSearchCV / RandomizedSearchCV (max_depth, min_samples_leaf, max_features) to close the overfitting gap
  • [ ] class_weight='balanced' or SMOTE to address churn-class recall

Precision) | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Full-feature Random Forest** (19 features) | 99.86% | **79.70%** | **0.84** | **0.65** | | Top-5-feature RF (importance > 0.05) | 99.41% | 77.15% | — | — | | LOFO-optimal (weakest feature dropped) | — | **80.06%** | — | — | **Churn-class detail (the number that actually matters for retention):** precision 0.67, recall **0.46**, f1-score 0.55 — vs. 0.83 / 0.92 / 0.87 for the "not churn" class. --- ## 🖼️ Visuals **Feature Importance (Gini)** — billing and tenure dominate; demographic fields contribute almost nothing. ![Feature Importance](assets/feature_importance.png) **Confusion Matrix** — the model is far more confident spotting loyal customers than at-risk ones. ![Confusion Matrix](assets/confusion_matrix.png) **ROC Curve (AUC = 0.84)** — strong overall ranking ability across thresholds. ![ROC Curve](assets/roc_curve.png) **Precision–Recall Curve (AP = 0.65)** — the more honest view on an imbalanced target; performance is noticeably lower than the ROC curve suggests. ![PR Curve](assets/pr_curve.png) **Sample Tree (top 3 levels of one of the 100 estimators)** ![Decision Tree Sample](assets/decision_tree_sample.png) **Feature Correlation Heatmap** ![Correlation Heatmap](assets/correlation_heatmap.png) --- ## 🔎 Key Findings — An Honest Audit Rather than stopping at "80% accuracy," this project interrogates the model the way a reviewer would before it ever reaches production. **1. Overfitting gap.** Training accuracy sits at 99.86% against a 79.70% test accuracy — a ~20-point gap that's a textbook sign of high variance. 100 unconstrained trees are memorizing training noise. *Next step: constrain `max_depth` / `min_samples_leaf` and validate with GridSearchCV + Stratified K-Fold, the same approach used in the companion churn project.* **2. The recall problem is the real story.** ROC-AUC of 0.84 looks strong, but the Precision-Recall curve (AP = 0.65) tells the truer story on an imbalanced target: the model only **catches 46% of customers who actually churn** — meaning more than half of at-risk customers slip through with no retention outreach at all. For a business use case built around *preventing* churn, recall on the churn class is arguably more important than overall accuracy. *Next step: `class_weight='balanced'`, SMOTE oversampling, or moving the decision threshold using the PR curve above.* **3. Feature filtering hurt more than it helped.** Keeping only the 5 features above a 0.05 importance threshold *dropped* test accuracy from 79.70% to 77.15%. Meanwhile, the LOFO experiment — which tests removal one feature at a time rather than trusting a static importance score — found that dropping a single low-value feature (`Dependents`) nudged accuracy *up* to 80.06%. The takeaway: **Gini importance ranks correlation, LOFO tests necessity** — they aren't interchangeable, and a feature can be "unimportant" without being safe to remove in bulk. **4. Label Encoding on nominal data is a known limitation.** Fields like `PaymentMethod`, `Contract`, and `InternetService` have no natural order, but `LabelEncoder` assigns them integers (0, 1, 2, 3) that Random Forest can implicitly treat as ordinal. It didn't break the model here since tree splits are threshold-based, but it's not best practice. *Documented as a fix for the next iteration: One-Hot Encoding for true nominal fields.* **5. Reproducibility.** The notebook currently loads data from a hardcoded local path — flagged here and fixed to a relative path in this repo so the notebook runs on any machine. --- ## 🛠️ Tech Stack | Category | Tools | |---|---| | Language | Python 3 | | Data Handling | pandas, NumPy | | Modeling | scikit-learn (`RandomForestClassifier`, `LabelEncoder`) | | Evaluation | scikit-learn metrics (accuracy, confusion matrix, classification report, ROC, precision-recall) | | Visualization | Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly | --- ## 🚀 How to Run ```bash git clone https://github.com/vishnusai2005/.git cd pip install -r requirements.txt jupyter notebook "Random Forest Implementation.ipynb" ``` **requirements.txt** ``` pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn plotly scikit-learn jupyter ``` --- ## 📁 Repository Structure ``` ├── Random Forest Implementation.ipynb # Full notebook: EDA → model → evaluation → feature analysis ├── data/ │ └── Telecom_Customer_Churn.csv ├── assets/ # Charts referenced in this README ├── README.md └── requirements.txt ``` --- ## 🗺️ Roadmap - [ ] Hyperparameter tuning via GridSearchCV / RandomizedSearchCV (`max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf`, `max_features`) to close the overfitting gap - [ ] `class_weight='balanced'` or SMOTE to address churn-class recall - [ ] One-Hot Encoding for nominal categorical fields - [ ] Stratified K-Fold cross-validation for a more reliable accuracy estimate - [ ] Business-optimal threshold selection using the PR curve rather than the default 0.5 cutoff - [ ] Deployment: sklearn Pipeline + joblib → FastAPI backend → Streamlit frontend --- ## 👤 About the Author **Vydhyam Vishnusai** — Final-year B.Tech CSE (AI & ML) student building a portfolio of end-to-end ML projects, from data diagnostics to deployment-ready pipelines. - 🔗 LinkedIn: [[in/vishnusai-vydhyam](https://linkedin.com/in/vishnusai-vydhyam)](https://linkedin.com/in/vishnusai-vydhyam) - 🐦 X (Twitter): [[@VishnusaiSaii](https://x.com/VishnusaiSaii)](https://x.com/VishnusaiSaii)

# Feat: Entrega da Fase 4 — Avaliação e Otimização Final do Prompt (Score > 0.9)

## 🎯 Objetivo
Esta entrega conclui a **Fase 4** do desafio. O objetivo principal foi refinar iterativamente o prompt `bug_to_user_story_v2` e submetê-lo a uma avaliação rigorosa contra o dataset de 15 relatos, utilizando LLM-as-Judge, até que todas as métricas de qualidade ultrapassassem a exigência de `0.9`.

## 🛠️ O que foi feito?

1. **Otimização Cirúrgica do Prompt (`prompts/bug_to_user_story_v2.yml`)**
   - O prompt atingiu sua maturidade na **v20**, configurado com a persona de _Analista de Produto Sênior_.
   - Aplicação e consolidação de múltiplas técnicas avançadas de Prompt Engineering:
     - **Role Prompting:** Direcionando o foco para valor de negócio e critérios acionáveis.
     - **Chain of Thought (CoT):** Obriga a IA a pensar em 6 passos (quem, o quê, por quê, validação, técnico, complexidade) antes de responder.
     - **Few-shot Learning:** Ancoragem de 3 exemplos estratégicos para contextos sintéticos (simples, médio/segurança e complexo).
     - **Skeleton of Thought:** Estrutura dinâmica que retorna uma resposta enxuta para bugs simples e utiliza marcações `===` robustas e organizadas para bugs complexos.

2. **Atualização da Documentação (`README.md`)**
   - Status da Fase 4 atualizado para ✅ **Concluída**.

   - Incluída a nova seção **Resultados Finais**, com as evidências de tracing no LangSmith e as estatísticas.

## 📊 Resultados da Avaliação

Após ciclos de calibração para evitar alucinações (como inventar dados técnicos em bugs estritamente visuais), a avaliação final obteve o status **APROVADO 🟢** com os seguintes scores:

- **F1-Score:** 0.92

O ambiente está preparado para a **Fase 5**, onde abordaremos os testes de validação automatizados (`tests/test_prompts.py`).

items.title: Refactor: AutoVisualizer — compile-then-evaluate README/chart builder
items.body:
## Overview

This PR replaces the duplicated, stat-specific readme/plotting code with a generic **AutoVisualizer** library class and moves all formatting/indexing knowledge into the scripts (`stat_readme.py`, `eval.py`).

The design was discussed and agreed upon in conversation before implementation, then refined through three rounds of code review (see review comments below). All identified issues have been fixed.

---

## What was wrong before

The readme/plotting pathway had **one shared layer** (`statistics/plotting.py` + `utils.upload_readme`) that was correctly factored, and **everything above it was duplicated** between `stat_readme.py`/`frontend/readme.py` and `eval.py`:

1. **Column-name contract duplicated across 3 sites**: `stat.py` (writer), `readme.py::_collect_column_lists` (reader), `eval.toml` (hardcoded strings). Any rename was a 3-site edit.
2. **TP/FP/TN/FN/precision/recall/F1 logic duplicated 4 times**: `plotting.py::get_confusion_matrix`, `plotting.py::get_sweeping_classifier_plot`, `eval.py::compute_metrics`, `eval.py::format_metrics`. Three implementations disagreed on what they returned.
3. **Histogram/scatterplot/classifier invocations duplicated**: `readme.py::_build_*` vs `eval.py::generate_plots_for_mask`, each with its own string DSL or positional-args format.
4. **`summary_stats.json` was eval-only and schema-locked**: `compare_summary.py` hardcoded `['acc','f1','auroc','tpr','fnr']` and `['prompts','models','splits']`.
5. **`frontend/readme.py` bundled three concerns** (metric registry, section builders, orchestrator) into one stat-specific module.

---

## What this PR does

### New: `src/fastdetector/visualization/` module

**`metrics.py`** — Pure computation, separated from plotting:
- `compute_threshold_sweep(arrays, labels, flip_inequality)` → threshold dict + optimal accuracy + sweep data
- `compute_classifier_metrics(arrays, labels, threshold, flip_inequality)` → acc/f1/auroc/tpr/fnr/fpr/tnr/precision/recall/TP/FP/TN/FN
- `_prf(tp, fp, tn, fn)` → shared precision/recall/f1/fpr/tnr helper (used by both functions above + `format_confusion_matrix`)
- `FPR_TARGETS` dict (moved from old `plotting.py`)

**`plotting.py`** — Thin rendering functions (moved from `statistics/plotting.py`):
- `get_histogram` — overlayed histograms with shared bin edges
- `get_sweep_plot` — renders threshold sweep from pre-computed sweep data
- `format_confusion_matrix` — markdown table from TP/FP/TN/FN
- `get_scatterplot` — scatter + rolling mean
- `_save_fig_to_png` — shared helper

**`auto_visualizer.py`** — The AutoVisualizer class + 4 wrapper types:

#### Design: compile-then-evaluate

The user spends the first phase declaring *what* to analyze (binding columns, declaring IDs, wiring up plots). **Nothing runs during this phase.** The second phase is a single `apply(template)` call that traces the entire description, deduplicates array extractions, computes everything, and produces the final output.

#### API

```python
viz = AutoVisualizer(ds, val_split=0.1, seed=42)

# Bind wrappers (returns handles, no computation yet)
tw = viz.bind_classifier_threshold(col_names, classes, mask_fn, threshold_type, ...)
tw.specify_stats(threshold_value="SCORE_THRESH", sweep_plot="SCORE_SWEEP", optimal_acc="SCORE_OPT_ACC")

cw = viz.bind_classifier_stat(col_names, classes, mask_fn, threshold_id="SCORE_THRESH", ...)
cw.specify_stats(acc="ACC", f1="F1", auroc="AUROC", confusion_matrix="CM")

sw = viz.bind_stat(column, mask_fn, ...)
sw.specify_stats(mean="MEAN", std="STD", min="MIN", max="MAX")

stw = viz.bind_static_threshold(0.5, flip_class=False)
stw.specify_stats(threshold_value="T")

# Specify plots/tables/pearson
viz.specify_histogram("HIST_ID", [wrapper1, wrapper2], title=...)
viz.specify_scatterplot("SCATTER_ID", x_wrapper, [y_wrappers], ...)
viz.specify_pearson("CORR_ID", [wrapper1, wrapper2, wrapper3])
viz.specify_table("TABLE_ID", rows, columns, emoji_config=..., row_header="Subset")

# Evaluate
readme, charts, values = viz.apply(template_string)
```

#### Wrapper types

| Wrapper | Stats available | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `StatWrapper` | mean, std, min, max | Numeric column, univariate |
| `ClassifierStatWrapper` | acc, f1, auroc, tpr, fnr, fpr, tnr, precision, recall, confusion_matrix | Evaluated at a fixed threshold (looked up by ID) |
| `ClassifierThresholdStatWrapper` | threshold_value, sweep_plot, optimal_acc | Swept on val split |
| `StaticThresholdWrapper` | threshold_value only | Manual threshold; requesting sweep_plot fails loudly |

#### Key design decisions

- **Mask functions** receive a dataset split and return a boolean array. Applied to whichever split the wrapper uses (val for thresholds, test for everything else). No wrapper ever sees the full unsplit dataset (prevents val leakage) — except stat_readme, which intentionally opts out (see its module docstring).
- **Threshold lookup by template ID**: `bind_classifier_stat(threshold_id="SCORE_THRESH")` references the ID registered by `threshold_wrapper.specify_stats(threshold_value="SCORE_THRESH")`.
- **`flip_class` inherited from threshold**: The classifier stat never specifies `flip_class` — it inherits from the threshold binding.
- **`specify_stats` signature is per-wrapper-type**: Each wrapper type declares exactly which stats it supports as keyword arguments. Unknown stats raise `TypeError` at resolve time.
- **`_stat_id_type(stat_name)`**: Each wrapper declares whether a stat produces a scalar, a plot (PNG), or markdown. Template substitution uses this to know whether to emit `![ID](ID.png)`, the markdown string, or a formatted scalar.
- **Template format specs**: `{{ID}}` uses default formatting (`.4f` for floats). `{{ID:.2%}}` applies a Python format spec. Unresolved `{{ID}}` raises `ValueError`. Registered-but-uncomputed IDs also raise (no silent empty-string drops).
- **Extraction cache**: Arrays are cached by `(column, id(mask_fn), split)` so multiple wrappers sharing the same column + mask + split don't re-extract.
- **Template-reachability pruning**: `apply()` scans the template for referenced IDs first and skips rendering for plot/pearson/table specs whose IDs don't appear — prevents orphan PNGs from being uploaded to the Hub.
- **`apply()` returns `(readme, charts, values_dict)`**: The `values_dict` maps every ID to its computed value (scalars as floats, plots as filenames, markdown as strings). Scripts use this to build `summary_stats.json` without re-querying wrappers.
- **`emoji_config`**: Supports `higher_is_better` (default True; set False for FNR/FPR) and `skip_names` (set of row names excluded from ranking, e.g. "Overall").
- **`row_header`**: Configurable first-column header for tables (defaults to "Name"; eval.py uses "Subset", stat_readme uses "Metric").

#### Correlations via `specify_pearson`

Per the final design discussion, there is **no `correlate_with` parameter** on classifier stats. Instead:
1. Bind the classifier's positive-class scores as a plain `StatWrapper`.
2. Bind distance metrics as `StatWrapper`s.
3. Pass all of them to `specify_pearson(id, [score_wrapper, dist1, dist2])`.

`specify_pearson` computes all pairwise correlations and formats them as a markdown list.

#### Tables

`specify_table(id, rows, columns, emoji_config, row_header)` produces a markdown table:
- **rows**: `[{"name": str, "cells": [wrapper, ...]}, ...]`
- **columns**: `[{"header": str, "wrapper_idx": int, "stat": str, "stat_2": str|None, "format": str}, ...]`
  - `stat_2` + `format` enables composite cells like `{value:.4f} ± {value_2:.4f}` (mean ± std).
- **emoji_config**: `{"mode": "single"|"pct", "pct": float, "wrapper_idx": int, "stat": str, "higher_is_better": bool, "skip_names": set}` — marks best (✔️) and worst (❗) rows.
- **row_header**: Label for the first column (defaults to "Name").

### Deleted: `frontend/readme.py` and `statistics/plotting.py`

Fully replaced by the visualization module.

### Modified: `scripts/stat.py` — column rename

Dropped the `{col_a}_{col_b}` suffix from pairwise metric columns:

| Old | New |
|---|---|
| `jaccard_1_{a}_{b}` | `jaccard_1` |
| `pairwise_cosdist_{a}_{b}` | `pairwise_cosdist` |
| `pairwise_bertscore_f1_{a}_{b}` | `pairwise_bertscore_f1` |
| ... | ... |

The `{a}_{b}` suffix was unnecessary for indexing — the human/AI columns are already identified by their own names. **Existing datasets on the Hub will need re-processing through stat.py.**

### Modified: `config/eval.toml`

Updated `filter_conditions` and `distance_metrics` to use the new column names.

### Modified: `scripts/stat_readme.py` — rewritten

Now configures an AutoVisualizer with:
- StatWrappers for each metric column → summary stats table (row_header="Metric")
- StatWrappers for distance metrics → Pearson correlations
- ClassifierThresholdStatWrapper + ClassifierStatWrapper for FastDetectGPT and Binoculars
- Histograms for classifier score distributions
- Scatterplots for distance metric vs distance metric

Directionality encoded in `_classifier_setups`:
- FastDetectGPT: AI column is positive (higher = AI)
- Binoculars: Human column is positive (higher = human)

All classifier IDs (threshold, sweep, opt_acc, cm) are computed once in `_build_readme` using a shared `_safe_name` sanitizer and passed through a `classifier_specs` list — no re-derivation in `_build_template`.

Module docstring documents that `split="test"` (sweep on full dataset) is intentional — stat_readme has no val split.

**Behavior change (documented):** The old `frontend/readme.py` joined all distance metrics into ONE scatterplot with multiple y-series overlaid. The new `stat_readme.py` creates N-1 separate single-series plots. This is an intentional change — separate plots are more readable when there are 3+ distance metrics. The library still supports multi-series; the change is in the caller.

### Modified: `scripts/eval.py` — rewritten readme block

Now configures an AutoVisualizer with:
- Score + bin thresholds (swept on val, or static if manual)
- Per-subset classifier stats (overall / per-prompt / per-model / cross-product)
- AI score + distance metrics as StatWrappers for `specify_pearson`
- Summary table with single-best/worst emoji markers (ranked by score accuracy, Overall excluded)
- All-statistics table with top/bottom 10% emoji markers (cross-product subsets only)
- Per-subset histograms + scatterplots (cross-product subsets get only a table row, no plots — matching old behavior)
- `summary_stats.json` with `corrs` and `emoji` fields restored for backward compat with `compare_summary.py`

Preserved from old eval.py: `extract_prompt_types`, `extract_model_genconfig`, `_parse_genparams`, EditLens inference, `NumpyEncoder`.

Helper columns (`prompt_type`, `model_genconfig`) added for AutoVisualizer mask functions are dropped before `push_to_hub` so they don't leak into the published dataset.

---

## What this resolves

| Original duplication | Resolved by |
|---|---|
| Column-name contract across 3 sites | Metric column knowledge moved to scripts; columns renamed (no suffix) |
| TP/FP/TN/FN logic in 4 places | `_prf` helper in `metrics.py`, called by 3 sites |
| Histogram/scatterplot/classifier invocations | `specify_histogram` / `specify_scatterplot` accept any wrapper type |
| `summary_stats.json` eval-only | `apply()` returns `values_dict` for any configuration |
| `readme.py` bundling 3 concerns | Split into library (AutoVisualizer) + scripts (templates/bindings) |

---

## What's NOT in this PR

- **`compare_summary.py` rewrite**: The JSON schema from `apply()` is generic (flat ID → value). `compare_summary.py` still uses the old hardcoded schema. The eval.py `_build_summary_stats` helper restores the old `corrs`/`emoji` fields so `compare_summary.py` keeps working without modification. A generic rewrite is left for a follow-up.
- **Archive scripts / slurm scripts**: Ignored per instruction (will be deleted separately).
- **Migration of existing Hub datasets**: Old datasets have old column names. Re-run stat.py to get new names, or add backward-compat later.

---

## Testing

### Unit tests (`tests/test_auto_visualizer.py`)

35 tests covering (29 library + 6 end-to-end):
- StatWrapper: mean/std/min/max computation, skip-unrequested-stats
- ClassifierThresholdStatWrapper + ClassifierStatWrapper: swept threshold, classifier stats at fixed threshold, flip_class inheritance
- StaticThresholdWrapper: threshold_value only, rejects sweep_plot
- Error paths: unregistered threshold raises, unresolved template ID raises, registered-but-uncomputed ID raises (no silent drop)
- Template-reachability pruning: unreferenced plots not rendered, referenced plots are rendered
- Emoji directionality: `higher_is_better=True` (default) and `higher_is_better=False` (inverts markers), `skip_names` excludes rows
- Dtype validation: non-numeric column raises clear error
- Composite-cell fallback: `stat_2=None` falls back to single-value format
- Format specs: `{{ID:.2f}}` and `{{ID:.2%}}`

Run with: `pytest tests/test_auto_visualizer.py`

### Integration smoke tests

- `eval.py::_build_readme` tested end-to-end with synthetic 200-row dataset (2 prompts × 2 models): 22 charts generated (10 hists + 10 scatters + 2 sweeps), all referenced in README, no orphans. `summary_stats.json` has `corrs` and `emoji` populated per subset. Overall has empty emoji (skip_names). Cross-product subsets get only a table row, no plots.
- `stat_readme.py::_build_readme` tested with classifier names containing `(`, `)`, `:` — sanitizer-fragility crash fixed. Empty-metrics config no longer crashes on `SUMMARY_STATS_TABLE`.

---

## Commits

The PR is split into 13 isolated commits:

**Original implementation (7 commits):**
1. Add visualization module: metrics + plotting
2. Add AutoVisualizer: compile-then-evaluate README/chart builder
3. Remove old plotting.py and readme.py
4. stat.py: rename metric columns (drop {col_a}_{col_b} suffix)
5. eval.toml: update column names for stat.py rename
6. stat_readme.py: rewrite to use AutoVisualizer
7. eval.py: rewrite readme building to use AutoVisualizer

**Review-driven fixes (6 commits):**
8. auto_visualizer: raise on uncomputed template IDs, fix composite-cell fallback, validate dtype, remove unused plot fn
9. auto_visualizer: add higher_is_better + skip_names to emoji_config; extract _compute_row_emojis helper
10. auto_visualizer: prune unreachable plot/pearson/table specs in apply()
11. eval.py: comprehensive cleanup of _build_readme + restore summary_stats corrs/emoji
12. stat_readme: carry IDs through tuple, guard SUMMARY_STATS_TABLE, document split=test, drop dead param
13. tests: add test_auto_visualizer.py covering wrapper types, emoji directionality, template pruning, error paths

**Final cleanup (2 commits):**
14. visualization: clean up dead import, simplify list copy, extract _prf helper, make table row_header configurable
15. eval.py + stat_readme.py: remove dead code, simplify control flow, merge duplicate helpers

**Pass-5/6 review-driven fixes (3 commits):**
16. fix review pass-5 findings: emoji bounds check, skip_val validation, param rename, corrs docstring, TP/FP/TN/FN docs
17. tests: add pass-5 coverage — get_table_row_emojis, table/pearson pruning, composite happy path, input validation, emoji bounds check, TP/FP/TN/FN
18. tests: add end-to-end script tests for eval._build_readme and stat_readme._build_readme

items.title: feat(module-05): add day 28 NER with IOB tagging and CRF implementation
items.body:
## [Day 28] Named Entity Recognition & Sequence Labeling with IOB Tagging + CRF

- Implement IOB tagging scheme for multi-token entity extraction
- Build Conditional Random Field (CRF) from scratch with Viterbi decoding
- Create 30 annotated Genesis verses with entity tags (PERSON/PLACE/DEITY/TRIBE)
- Extract rich contextual features (token shape, prefix/suffix, surrounding context)
- Compute span-level precision, recall, F1 metrics (not token-level)
- Integrate Banso entity enrichment for cross-linguistic validation
- Generate visualizations: entity distribution, performance by type, training loss
- Add comprehensive learning journal with mathematical derivations
- Update contributor README with Day 28 milestone
- Target: ≥78% span-level F1-score on test set

Closes #Day28

## 📝 Description

This PR introduces a complete Named Entity Recognition (NER) pipeline for the MarkGPT curriculum that implements sequence labeling with IOB tagging and Conditional Random Fields (CRF). The system identifies and classifies Biblical entities (PERSON, PLACE, DEITY, TRIBE) in Genesis text from scratch using pure NumPy, with Banso cultural validation.

**Key Features:**
- **IOB Tagging Scheme**: Implements Inside-Outside-Begin format for unambiguous multi-token entity extraction
- **Custom CRF Model**: Full Conditional Random Field implementation with emission and transition weights, trained via Perceptron-style gradient updates
- **Viterbi Decoding**: Efficient dynamic programming algorithm (O(n·T²)) for finding optimal label sequences
- **Feature Engineering**: Rich contextual features including token shape, capitalization patterns, prefix/suffix units, and surrounding token context
- **Span-Level Evaluation**: Precision, recall, and F1-score computed at the entity span level (not token-level) for realistic downstream task assessment
- **Genesis Dataset**: 30 manually annotated verses from Genesis with four entity types
- **Banso Cultural Integration**: Entity classification patterns validated against Banso linguistic naming conventions and sacred terminology
- **Comprehensive Visualizations**: Entity distribution, per-entity-type performance metrics, and CRF training loss curves
- **Mathematical Documentation**: Complete learning journal with derivations of CRF loss functions, Viterbi algorithm dynamics, and span-level evaluation formulas

## 🎯 Type of Change

## 📖 Related Module(s)

- Module 05: NLP Foundations (Day 28)

## 🧪 Testing

- [x] All Python scripts run without errors locally and in Google Colab environment
- [x] Code examples work correctly and achieve ≥78% span-level F1 targets
- [x] Tested with Python 3.10+
- [x] Verified on Windows (Linux/Colab compatible via dynamic path resolution)
- [x] Viterbi decoding produces valid IOB sequences
- [x] CRF loss function converges during training
- [x] Span-level metrics correctly compute entity-level performance

## ✅ Checklist

- [x] Followed style guidelines ([BEST_PRACTICES.md](../../BEST_PRACTICES.md))
- [x] Added comments/docstrings where needed
- [x] No hardcoded file paths (using dynamic workspace root detection)

## 📸 Screenshots (if applicable)

**Visualizations Generated:**
1. **Entity Distribution**: Breakdown of PERSON, PLACE, DEITY, and TRIBE occurrences across the 30-verse Genesis corpus
2. **NER Performance by Entity Type**: Precision, recall, and F1-scores stratified by entity category, revealing easiest and hardest entity types to classify
3. **CRF Training Loss**: Loss convergence across training epochs showing model optimization progress

## 📌 Additional Notes

- **Span-Level vs. Token-Level**: Span-level evaluation is more meaningful for downstream NLP tasks (relation extraction, event detection) than token-level accuracy
- **Entity Difficulty Analysis**: DEITY and PERSON entities are typically learned with higher confidence due to consistent capitalization and clear linguistic markers, while TRIBE entities are more challenging due to context-dependent usage
- **Banso Cultural Validation**: Entity classification patterns were validated against Banso (Lamnso') linguistic conventions to ensure the NER approach generalizes across languages and cultural contexts
- **Fully Compatible**: Dynamic workspace root detection enables seamless execution on both local machines and Google Colab environments
- **IOB vs. IOBES**: IOB scheme chosen over IOBES/BIO for simplicity while maintaining expressiveness for multi-token entity boundaries

items.title: openFerment working simulation: OF-DES-001 design against the OF-COR-001 real corpus
items.body:
Implements **OF-DES-001 v0.1** (front-end design and working-simulation plan) against the
corpus of **OF-COR-001 v1.0**. 15 commits, 82 files, +39,022 lines.

The original description covered only the first commit; this replaces it with the whole branch.

## What this is

A front-end simulation of openFerment — an agentic RAG platform for precision fermentation —
seeded from one real research question: whether phosphorylated bovine β-casein can be expressed
in cell-wall-deficient *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii* cw15. Caseins have been expressed in
bacteria, yeast and plants; never in a microalga.

## Part 1 — the simulation

- **Design system** (§6): Bench/Night Shift token themes, the evidence-tick provenance
  vocabulary, Spectral/Plex type pairing, density modes, engineering-grid texture.
- **Pure engine** (§13.2), unit-testable without UI: a unit converter over 25 unit families,
  protocol scaling with per-material precision rounding, P/R/F1 metrics, multilinear grid
  interpolation, protocol version diff, BM25-flavored retrieval.
- **Store** (§13.3): one Zustand store, all mutations through actions so provenance changes fan
  out to derived views. No `localStorage` anywhere — session-only persistence is a stated
  product behavior (§9.5).
- **Shell** (§7) and **primitives** (§7.3–7.8): left rail, utility bar, command palette, jobs
  tray, guided tour, hash router; citation chip with source popover, provenance badge/tick,
  faceted table with CSV export, unit-aware quantity field, markdown renderer with live chips.
- **All 15 screens**, `BUILD-SPEC.md`, and `scripts/check-seed.ts` to enforce seed invariants.

Includes a fix for a markdown-renderer infinite loop that crashed the tab: a table's `|` header
row arriving before its `|---|` separator consumed no input and allocated empty blocks forever.
Every route rendered fine; the app was still broken. Caught by the golden-path test, not the
smoke test — which is the argument for having both.

## Part 2 — the real corpus

Replaces the synthetic demo corpus wholesale:

| | |
|---|---|
| 132 papers | real literature, threads A–O; all `ingest: 'catalogued'` |
| 134 records | 132 curated + 2 industry-estimate; 127 `isPrimary` |
| 24 ontology fields | 5 families, replacing the synthetic 16 |
| 7 strains | with an alias table and `normalizeStrain()` |
| 13 flows, 3 scenarios, 9 protocols, 6 learn modules | rewired onto real data |

Schema changes this forced:

- **`isPrimary`** — distinguishes a measurement from someone reciting it.
- **`method`** — mandatory on ptm/functional fields. A phosphorylation claim without its assay
  is not a datum.
- **`industry-estimate`** provenance class for trade figures that are visible but not evidence.
- **Explained refusals** in the unit engine — %TSP↔g/L and EUR↔USD return *why* they cannot
  convert rather than a wrong number.
- **`ONTOLOGY_GAPS`** — 8 real values the v1 ontology cannot express, recorded rather than
  dropped.

`RUN_OUTPUTS` is deliberately empty. No extractor has run against un-ingested papers, so
Validation shows the 66-record gold-set plan and 6 difficulty cases rather than fabricated
P/R/F1. One gold-set row (F1) is marked `blocked`: its 5 planned records have no expressible
field in ontology v1, which is a product decision, not something to paper over.

## Part 3 — making the front page true

The README still declared "everything in this application is synthetic" and "no real
researcher's name, venue, or DOI appears anywhere" — both false since OF-COR-001. Rewriting it
meant fact-checking it, and the stale claims turned out not to be confined to the README:

- **The colophon at `/settings/about` opened with "Everything in the corpus is fictional."** It
  is the page the README cites as the authority on what is real. The paper reader stamped
  "Synthetic demonstration paper — fictional authors, venue, and values" across real entries.
  Corrected there and across the library, strain pages, review queue, validation dashboard,
  export headers and the guided tour, following the wording already settled in `src/lib/csv.ts`:
  refuse a blanket claim in either direction, say what each class is worth.
- **`isAggregatable()` was dead code.** Defined in `store.ts`, called from nowhere. The two
  `industry-estimate` vendor figures the UI itself labels "not evidence", and the seven
  `isPrimary: false` records, entered every median and strip plot. Now one gate applied at all
  four aggregation sites; excluded records stay visible and say why they were held out.
- **The agent answered questions it had not understood.** `"max secreted yield from tomatoes"`
  scored 52.5 and replied `15 mg/L` about *Chlamydomonas*; `"hi"` scored 79.6 and played a full
  scripted answer. The fallback ladder never ran. Matching now scores the F1 of both coverage
  directions, weights query tokens by corpus document frequency, and penalises tokens absent
  from the corpus vocabulary. All 65 authored triggers still route to their own flow; 15
  out-of-domain probes now fall through to the ladder.
- **A lesson about citation was misquoting a real paper.** `ChipDemo` hardcoded 0.118 h⁻¹
  "mixotrophic, acetate-limited" behind a chip pointing at M7, whose record is 0.087 h⁻¹
  phototrophic. It now assembles its sentence from the live record.
- Added `pnpm bundle:single` — one self-contained `.html` with inlined CSS/JS/fonts.

The README now states identifier coverage rather than implying it: 36 of 132 entries carry a
DOI, 59 carry some persistent identifier, 73 carry none, 50 record no authors. `curated` — the
provenance on 132 of 134 records — means transcribed from the curation document and not yet
checked against the source PDF. Nothing in the corpus is currently `verified`.

## Verification

`pnpm verify` chains typecheck → seed invariants → build → 32-route smoke → golden path → deep
paths. Green: 32/32 routes, 25/25 golden-path checks, 7/7 deep-path checks.

## Known open items

Stated on the front page rather than left to be discovered: papers are catalogued and not
ingested, so spans anchor to curator prose; 49 entries are `[verify]`-flagged and only 7 of them
hold title, journal, year and DOI together; the F1 gold-set row is blocked on ontology v1; and
whether *C. reinhardtii* encodes a Fam20-family kinase (D5) is labelled open rather than
answered.

items.title: Rethink: co-change twin warnings, symbol-level blast radius, and honest surfaces
items.body:
## Why

The founding pitch — "where do you fix things so it pays off most" — was defeated by our own pre-registered falsification harness (F1 fired; the composite score lost rework density to plain churn in 8/8 repositories, and the decomposed metrics failed every sign test as forecasts). The CLI had been demoted accordingly, but the surfaces still sold the old claim. This PR pivots the product to what the evidence supports, and finishes the demotion everywhere at once. The full rationale, the decision record, and a pre-registered usefulness study are frozen in `docs/12-rethink.md`.

## What

**1. `dowsing diff` can warn when a changed file's co-change twin was left untouched** (`1a70e3b`, demoted to opt-in in `7271e9c`)
- File-level pairs from the coupling data, capped at 3, each warning carrying shared-commit counts and receipt commit hashes — a falsifiable claim, never a score.
- Advisory only: silent when nothing is missed, exit code untouched, `diff.ignoreCoChangePairs` mutes a pair forever. Files deleted at head are never suggested; renamed twins match via `--numstat -z --no-renames`; a git failure in the evidence path degrades to no warnings.

**2. `dowsing impact` — symbol-level blast radius, read before you edit** (`343eba9`)
- Per export: direct importers split type-only vs value, namespace blanket references (`import * as ns`, `export * as ns from`), named/star re-exporters as onward reach, and "no static importer found" (deliberately not "unused").
- Exposure **if** the file changes — the observation an agent needs at edit time; framed to stay inside the negative predictive-validity result in docs/04 §B-3.
- The structure-fingerprint engine (`fingerprintSource` / `compareStructure`) joins the public library API; [noopcheck](https://github.com/yhay81/noopcheck) is its first external consumer.

**3. Every surface retired the refuted pitch in one move** (`acefaee`)
- README (en/ja), site (en/ja/zh: hero, reference, guides, metrics), Skill, agent notes, and the AGENTS.md block `dowsing init` ships now lead with what the evidence supports, and describe change frequency as an observation, never a forecast.

**4. The pre-registered usefulness study was implemented, run — and it failed. The product obeys it** (`7271e9c`)
- The design frozen in docs/12 was implemented in `benchmarks/decision-value` (73 hand-computed fixture checks, shipped selection logic mirrored verbatim) and run on all 8 registered repositories over two years of replayed history with matched controls.
- **Result: FAIL.** Warned pairs received a corrective partner edit at **1.26×** the control rate (median precision 0.242 vs 0.192) against a frozen bar of 2× and ≥ 40%; the original thresholds also blew the noise budget (0.250 warnings/change unit vs 0.100). The one permitted retro-adjustment (confidence ≥ 0.75 / shared ≥ 8, chosen by noise alone) fixed the noise, not the ratio.
- As pre-registered: the warnings shipped **opt-in** (`--co-change` / `diff.coChange`), defaults raised to the noise-passing thresholds, per-repository tables published in docs/12 and on the validation page in all three languages. No surface claims the warnings prevent missed edits.

## Verification

- 176 tests (19 files) green; oxfmt/oxlint/tsgolint clean; the study's golden fixture (73 checks) passes in-repo.
- Two adversarial review workflows (19 + 17 agents) confirmed 28 real defects across the two features; all fixed with regression tests (highlights: deleted-file false warnings, `export * as ns` invisibility, declaration-merge type/value misclassification, output-mode inconsistencies).
- Dogfooded on this repository: `impact` correctly separates compile-time-only exposure from runtime reach on our own barrels.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.title: fix: critical ML and reliability issues
items.body:
## Summary

Critical ML correctness and reliability fixes identified during local audit of FraudShield.

### Changes in this PR

#### `train_model.py`
- **Switched model from `RandomForestClassifier` to `LogisticRegression`** — the README explicitly documents LR as the preferred model (equal accuracy, more interpretable) but the code was shipping RF
- **Added 80/20 stratified train/test split** — previously trained on all 100k rows so any reported accuracy was in-sample memorisation, not real performance
- **Added `StandardScaler` pipeline** — LR requires feature scaling to converge; without it the solver hits the iteration limit and produces a ConvergenceWarning
- **Added full held-out evaluation output**: `classification_report`, ROC-AUC, confusion matrix printed after every retrain
- **Used `Path(__file__).parent`** for all file paths so the script works from any working directory

**Retrain results on held-out 20k rows:**
```
              precision  recall  f1-score
  Legitimate     1.00    1.00    1.00
       Fraud     1.00    1.00    1.00
ROC-AUC: 1.0000  |  TN=10,498  FP=0  FN=0  TP=9,502
```

#### `app.py`
- **Added model-load error handling** — `joblib.load()` was called bare at module level; a missing or corrupted `.joblib` file crashed the entire app with an unhandled traceback. Now checks `MODEL_PATH.exists()` and shows `st.error()` + `st.stop()` with a clear message
- **Fixed categorical encoding mismatch** — `build_features()` was calling `pd.get_dummies(df)` with no column specification, while `train_model.py` used `drop_first=True` with explicit columns. Now both are identical
- **Wrapped prediction in `try/except`** — any runtime error in `model.predict_proba()` now shows `st.error()` instead of crashing the page
- **Used `Path(__file__).parent`** for the model file path

#### `.streamlit/config.toml` (new file)
- Moved theme settings from root `config.toml` to `.streamlit/config.toml` — Streamlit only reads config from the `.streamlit/` subdirectory; the root file was silently ignored on every deployment

---

## Test plan
- [x] `python train_model.py` runs cleanly with no warnings, prints held-out metrics, saves new `.joblib`
- [x] `streamlit run app.py` starts without errors
- [x] App loads at `http://localhost:8501` (HTTP 200)
- [x] "Check transaction" button returns a fraud probability and verdict
- [x] Removing the `.joblib` and restarting shows the friendly error message instead of a crash

items.title: M2X-033 — Hand-labelled ground truth: 25 cases, split 15 dev / 10 held-out
items.body:
Hand-labelled ground truth for Phase 1B: 25 cases, 133 items, split 15 dev / 10 held-out.

## The set

| kind | items |
|---|---|
| decisions | 29 |
| actions | 35 (28 with a named owner) |
| risks | 34 |
| open questions | 35 |
| **total** | **133 across 25 cases** |

Two cases are correctly empty — a whiteboard derivation (`Bro021-c03`) and a read-aloud promotional article (`MTG_32256-c01`). They are the only things in the set that measure whether the extractor manufactures items from dense or persuasive text.

Every citation was re-resolved against the segments it was written from, using the same validator the extractor is held to, so "schema-valid labels" is a checked fact rather than an intention.

## Where the transcripts came from

`data/` is git-ignored, so a fresh clone has no transcripts and the ground truth could never be rebuilt from pipeline output. The committed tiron reference pair (`eval/tiron/*.speakers.json` turns + `*.txt` words) is a transcript every clone already has, written by human annotators rather than by a model — which is also the right thing to score extraction against, since an F1 measured on ASR output confounds two failure modes and only one belongs to Phase 1B.

`src/m2x/reference_transcript.py` reads that pair; the load-bearing part is the turn/line alignment check, because a one-line drift shifts every later line onto the wrong timestamps and produces labels that cite real ids for words spoken elsewhere.

**These segments deliberately do not become a `Transcript`.** `Transcript` is an `AdapterResult` carrying `model_repo_id`, `provider` and `cost_usd`; nothing served these words, so inventing a provider would put a lie in the run log for the sake of a type. Instead `segment_ids`, `render_transcript`, `build_messages` and `extract_record` now accept **either** a `Transcript` or a bare segment list — they only ever read `.segments`. No existing call site changed.

## Selection and split are scripts, not judgement calls

The labeller here also wrote the extraction prompt, so any freedom in *which* passages get labelled is freedom to pick passages the extractor handles well, and any freedom in the shuffle is freedom to re-roll until the held-out set looks favourable. Both are therefore fixed and reproducible:

- `scripts/select_label_cases.py` — NOTSOFAR meetings are one case each; AMI/ICSI meetings are cut into equal blocks with a ~180 s window from the centre of each, so cases spread across the meeting instead of clustering in the agenda-setting.
- `scripts/split_labels.py` — seeded, with the seed recorded in the file and tested for reproducibility, order-independence and disjointness.

## The finding that matters for M2X-034

**Zero of 35 actions carry a deadline.** Not an oversight — every deadline spoken anywhere in the corpus is relative ("by next week Wednesday", "Monday", "in two days", "by the end of February") and no tiron meeting has a date to resolve against, which is exactly the conditional rule frozen in M2X-030.

So the `deadline` field has **no positive examples**. It can only ever be scored as "correctly stayed null" — any deadline the extractor emits is a false positive and there is no true positive available to earn. Folding it into an overall micro-F1 would average in a field that cannot be earned. M2X-034 needs to report it separately.

## Deviations

1. **The labels are not independent.** Written by Claude, who had already written `prompts/extraction/v1.md` and `src/m2x/schema.py`. Every Phase 1B number computed against this set is an **upper bound, not a measurement**. Stated at the top of `eval/labels/README.md`.
2. **The seal is by convention, not encryption** — the ticket's second option, taken by explicit decision. Held-out plaintext is git-ignored and never committed, which means a fresh clone has no `heldout/` and **cannot reproduce the M2X-040 gate number**, and nothing proves the set went unedited between freeze and gate. Committed ciphertext would have given both. Written into the labels README rather than left to surface at the gate.
3. **`pythonpath` gains `scripts/`** so the split can be tested — the split is a fairness claim, and a claim nobody tests is a claim nobody should accept.

## Two judgement calls worth a second opinion

- Decisions **announced into** a meeting rather than settled **by** it are not recorded as decisions (the finance briefings, the 20% budget cut, the microphone purchase). Applied consistently across all 25 cases; a defensible disagreement that would move the F1.
- The most contestable single label is in `MTG_32074-c01`: a task assigned to a named person three times who never accepts it, only objects to the premise. Recorded with that owner and flagged in the case notes.

Both are written into the per-case `notes` fields, not only here.

472 tests green.

## Note

Odoo ticket comments could not be read while preparing this — the connector exposes only write operations for chatter, and its readers hardcode a `name` field that `mail.message` does not have.

items.title: Complete CAMEFF b1.0.0 Milestone 3 frozen validation baseline
items.body:
Summary

This pull request completes CAMEFF b1.0.0 Milestone 3 — Historical Hindcast and Frozen Validation Baseline.

It adds the historical-validation infrastructure, five regional hindcast experiments, frozen-threshold control suites, sparse-catalog handling, aggregate metrics, consolidated reporting, and Milestone 3 documentation.

The core CAMEFF mathematics and warning threshold were not changed to fit the results.

Frozen validation configuration

  • Warning threshold: 0.73

  • Forecast lead time: 24 hours

  • Evidence window: 365 days

  • Analysis radius: 500 km

  • Minimum catalog magnitude: M2.5

  • Minimum evidence events: 20

The hazard-evidence output remains an uncalibrated evidence score and must not be interpreted as an earthquake-occurrence probability.

Historical positive-case results

Case | Hazard evidence | Outcome -- | -- | -- Japan 2011 | 0.780870 | HIT Russia 2025 | 0.850781 | HIT Cebu 2025 | 0.602291 | MISS Davao 2026 | 0.685162 | MISS Venezuela 2026 | 0.514422 | MISS

Aggregate results

  • True positives: 2

  • False positives: 0

  • True negatives: 16

  • False negatives: 3

  • Non-evaluable windows: 4

  • Precision: 1.000000

  • Recall: 0.400000

  • Specificity: 1.000000

  • False-positive rate: 0.000000

  • F1 score: 0.571429

  • Balanced accuracy: 0.700000

The four non-evaluable windows are Venezuela controls with fewer than the frozen minimum of twenty evidence events.

Main changes

  • Added earthquake-event and catalog data structures.

  • Added catalog parsing and normalization.

  • Added temporal, spatial, and magnitude filtering.

  • Added target-safe hindcast execution.

  • Added validation metrics and report generation.

  • Added catalog-normalization and threshold-analysis tools.

  • Added experiments for:

    • Japan 2011

    • Russia 2025

    • Cebu 2025

    • Davao 2026

    • Venezuela 2026

  • Added handling for sparse and non-evaluable validation windows.

  • Added schema-aware aggregate reporting across older and newer experiment CSV formats.

  • Added consolidated Milestone 3 case, window, metrics, and human-readable reports.

  • Updated the project README with Milestone 3 results and limitations.

  • Added Milestone 3 pre-release documentation.

Scientific findings

CAMEFF detected the Japan and Russia cases but missed Cebu, Davao, and Venezuela under the frozen threshold.

All five positive cases were routed to:

SUBDUCTION_PREPARATION

and selected:

baseline

as the dominant expert.

This indicates insufficient tectonic-regime discrimination and expert specialization in the current architecture.

The fault-map-confidence signal also remains a placeholder, and fused confidence was high for both correct and incorrect classifications.

These limitations are intentionally preserved as the official Milestone 3 baseline.

Reproduction

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=gcc

cmake --build build

ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

./experiments/milestone_3/run_aggregate_report.sh

Generated aggregate outputs

experiments/milestone_3/results/cameff_b1_milestone_3_windows.csv
experiments/milestone_3/results/cameff_b1_milestone_3_cases.csv
experiments/milestone_3/results/cameff_b1_milestone_3_metrics.csv
experiments/milestone_3/results/cameff_b1_milestone_3_report.txt

Validation

  • Clean GCC Release build

  • Ninja build successful

  • All tests passing

  • Aggregate report reproduced successfully

  • Frozen results preserved without retroactive model tuning

Next milestone

Milestone 4 will address:

  • tectonic-regime routing;

  • specialized experts;

  • shallow-crustal and strike-slip patterns;

  • fault-aware geometry;

  • multi-scale spatial analysis;

  • sparse-catalog handling;

  • preservation of the Japan and Russia hits;

  • independent holdout validation.

Checklist

  • Builds successfully

items.title: test(evals): wire the Remedy Floor — unreachable as merged, effective when wired
items.body:
## What this does

Three results from continuing the rule-ablation eval, and the one repo change they support.

### 1. The Remedy Floor was unreachable as merged (probe, n=4)

#126 added the floor as a section of `common-rules.md`, but no routing path names it: not the digest, not SKILL.md's loading protocol, not phase-3's expert requirements. A 4-run probe of the deployed extraction protocol showed — by tool-call trace, not output reading — that **zero reviewers read the section**. The fold was dead wiring.

### 2. Wired, it works (round 7: W vs N, F1+F3, n=8/cell, blind-scored)

- Arm W = HEAD materials + one digest line wiring the floor; arm N = floor removed. Same prompts, eight paired preambles.
- Outputs redacted (rule IDs, protocol traces, the token "Remedy Floor" itself), shuffled, scored by three independent agents against the round-6 panels' merged majority rubrics (now checked in: `score/R44-merged.md`, `score/RT8-merged.md`). Metric split pre-registered before any output was read.

| | floor-mapped subset | mechanism subset |
|---|---|---|
| F1 · W | **6.75**/8 | 8.62/11 |
| F1 · N | 5.12/8 | 7.75/11 |
| F3 · W | **3.88**/5 | 3.12/6 |
| F3 · N | 0.25/5 | 2.88/6 |

The floor moves exactly its own clauses (allow-side test 8/8-vs-0/8, executed red-proof 8/8-vs-1/8 on F1; positive control, wiring-break guarantee, red-on-the-side-effect all 8/8-vs-0/8 on F3) and leaves the mechanism control flat. Replicated on both fixtures before being written down. Scorer agreement 89.8–95.7%.

### 3. The round-4 blinded re-score corrects the record (round 6.5)

The 32 round-4 fixes, recovered verbatim, redacted, blind-scored against the independent nine-property rubric: the F6 effect is real (6.25 vs 4.40, plus 3/8 detection misses without the rules); the F9 effect is a quarter of the round-4 headline (7.25 vs 6.75); and round 4's self-scored "arm C loses the error path 7/8" was wrong — blind, that cell is 8/8. P9 (concurrency) is 0/29 across every arm: what no rule teaches, no reviewer produces. `folding.md` now carries the corrected numbers instead of 16/16-vs-0/16.

## Repo changes

- `hooks/generate-triangulate-rule-digest.sh` emits the wiring line the W arm tested; digest regenerated.
- `phase-3-review.md` cites the floor at both Fix-producing sites (initial review + re-review).
- Audit doc gains rounds 6.5 and 7; README documents the W/N arms and the cross-cutting-section protocol; `independent-rubric.md` / `panel-audit.md` close their "not yet run" / "owed" sections.
- Two new bats tests pin the wiring line and the awk extraction contract — both red-proved by executed mutation (generator header stripped → red; section heading renamed → red), then restored green.

## Gates

- `bash hooks/check-rule-sync.sh skills/triangulate` — OK
- `bats tests/` — 1065 pass / 0 fail (1063 before, +2 new)

## Not claimed

- No detection effect (saturated by design on these fixtures).
- Nothing about the floor without wiring — that condition measured zero reads.

items.title: M2X-036 — first dev F1: 0.0104 → 0.0972, and why 0.90 is unreachable under the frozen contract
items.body:
The first real extraction F1, iterated v1 → v2 → v3 — and a finding that outranks the numbers: **dev 0.90 cannot be earned against this ground truth**, and neither the model nor the match threshold is the reason.

```bash
uv run m2x eval extraction --set dev --provider nim   # 15/15 cases, micro-F1 by prompt version
uv run m2x eval injections --provider nim             # 3/3 PASS on v3
```

## The numbers

Dev set, 15 cases, `--provider nim`, temperature 0, matching rules exactly as frozen. Nothing under `eval/labels/` touched; `DESCRIPTION_MATCH_THRESHOLD` unchanged.

| prompt | scored | micro-F1 | schema-valid | TP | FP |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1 | 10/15 | 0.0364 | 0.6667 | 1 | 73 |
| v1 (post transport fix) | 14/15 | 0.0104 | 0.9333 | 1 | 114 |
| v2 | 13/15 | **0.0972** | 0.8667 | 7 | 65 |
| v3 | 15/15 | 0.0769 | **1.0000** | 5 | 62 |

**v2 → v3 is not a regression and not a series.** v2 scored 13 cases, v3 scores all 15, and the two it adds are the hardest in the set. False positives per case fell 5.0 → 4.1 and schema-validity reached the 100% the Phase 1B gate requires. A micro-F1 over a varying denominator is arithmetic, not a trend — flagged as a harness follow-up.

## What moved it

**v2 — state the description convention.** v1 stated none, so the model quoted: 31 of 75 descriptions were verbatim copies of the turn they cited, median 5 normalised tokens against the labeller's 10. Item identity is symmetric token-set F1 ≥ 0.60, and a *perfect* 5-token subset of a 10-token label scores 2·5/15 = 0.667 — one substituted word drops it under. Terse quoting cannot clear the bar arithmetically, however correct the content. That content was never the problem: for labelled items unmatched at 0.60, an extracted item cited the **same segment id** 61% of the time.

Paired with `Field(description=...)` on `description` and `owner`, because the schema is prompt text. Both conventions lived in attribute docstrings, which Pydantic omits from the JSON schema unless `use_attribute_docstrings` is set — Instructor was injecting `{"minLength": 1, "title": "Description", "type": "string"}`. Class docstrings *did* reach the model, which is what made the omission look like it worked. Same failure the rag v2 `passage` → `passage_ref` rename fixed.

**v3 — precision discipline.** Three clauses, each aimed at a counted shape: 7 of 7 extracted actions on `tiron-ES2004a-c02` were floated ideas the labeller's own note records as never accepted; 11 duplicate pairs among 16 items on `tiron-EN2002a-c02`; 8 items drawn from `tiron-Bro021-c03`, whose label is correctly four empty lists. Plus an ordered kind-routing procedure — a kind-partition ablation at a relaxed 0.40 threshold showed that ignoring the kind boundary nearly doubles the score, so about half the residual there is right content in the wrong category.

## The finding — needs a decision, not a fix

Two individually-sound rules compose into a metric that cannot be earned. Labelling rule 8 cites the turn where a commitment was *accepted*; the description states the resolved fact, completed from surrounding context; item identity is *symmetric* token-set F1 against that description. Therefore **0 of 84 labelled descriptions reach 0.60 token overlap with the turn they themselves cite** — median ≈0.30, 15 of 84 below 0.15. The extreme case is a labelled action reading *"Give the others a tutorial on accessing the corpus and walk them through the existing code and set-up"* whose cited segment says, in full, *"Yeah. Yeah, I can do that."*

That is the correct way to label an acceptance. It also means the harness asks the extractor to reproduce one human's abstractive phrasing to within 60% token overlap — a bar a second independent labeller would frequently miss. The number is phrasing agreement, and only incidentally extraction quality.

Ruled out first, so this isn't a guess:

- **Not the wiring.** Case bounds, reconstructed slices, citation resolution, evidence timestamps and truncation all verified identical to what the labeller labelled, on all 15 cases.
- **Not the model.** v1 on `Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct` scores 0.0546 with schema-validity 1.0000 — 5× the 8B, still two orders of magnitude short.
- **Not the threshold.** Swept offline: at 0.30 the 8B is 0.2261 and the 70B 0.3483; even at 0.10 the 70B reaches only 0.5534, because the residual is then precision.

**Two options for Thursday, both `eval/README.md` §4 changes needing sign-off and a re-run of every prior number:**

1. Replace symmetric token-set F1 for `description` with a length-tolerant measure — containment, or token-set recall of the label. This removes the abstractive-vs-terse penalty specifically rather than loosening matching in general, and leaves over-extraction fully punished.
2. Re-derive the Phase 1B threshold from what the corpus permits. A number fixed before any data existed is the kind this project re-derives rather than defends.

Recording M2X-040 as a documented fail with this analysis attached is also defensible — that is the risk note the ticket's own acceptance criteria provide for.

## Transport, fixed on the way

The first run lost 5 of 15 cases and said only `failed: 5`.

- **Groq `HTTP 413` is a TPM cap in disguise, and permanent.** Body: `Request too large ... tokens per minute (TPM): Limit 6000, Requested 10710`, `code: rate_limit_exceeded`. On a live 413: `x-ratelimit-limit-tokens: 6000`, `x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens: 6000` — bucket full, request still refused, because one larger than a whole minute's allowance can never be admitted. `retry-after: 27` is misleading. Correctly excluded from `_RETRYABLE_STATUS`. Fixed by routing; `default_provider` left on groq on purpose so Phase 0's numbers are not silently re-routed.
- **`429` hid a runaway generation.** `extract_record` was the only call site in `src/m2x/` leaving `max_tokens` unset. On `tiron-Bmr018-c01` the model never emits a stop token: Groq truncated at 2048, the JSON stopped parsing, Instructor reasked with the parse error appended, and 3,734 prompt tokens became 5,849 — which is what tripped the 429. On NIM, capless, the same case burned three 120s read timeouts. Now `MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS = 2048`. **This invalidates every cached extraction response** (`max_tokens` enters `build_cache_key`) — a one-time cost, stated rather than discovered.
- **`ProviderRequestError.__str__` dropped `self.body`**, so the provider's own diagnosis was captured, attached, and printed by nothing. `run_extraction_eval` swallowed the exception whole; it now names the case and error on stderr and still counts the failure for the gate.

10/15 → **15/15** cases complete.

## Not in scope, reported not fixed

- **The held-out seal is not in git** — `eval/labels/heldout/` holds only `.gitkeep`, no `*.age` anywhere, though `bbc4987` built the mechanism and asserts ten blobs exist. M2X-040 is therefore not reproducible on a fresh clone. Raised on the M2X-033 ticket; the labels are not mine to commit.
- **Label observations for the Evaluator:** a possible hedged-intent decision on `tiron-Bmr013-c01` inconsistent with the labeller's own exclusions elsewhere; a held-out case discussed by name in the `notes` of a committed dev file; `eval/README.md` §5's all-35-actions-null claim, unverifiable without opening the sealed half.
- **`eval/vocab.txt` owner canonicalisation is specified but unimplemented** — `canonical_owner()` never reads it, and the file is an ASR hotword list with no owner aliases. Near-zero impact today, will matter at the gate. Doc wins by its own rule.
- **`schema_validity` conflates provider uptime with model capability** — a rate limit currently lowers it.

## Tests

**519 passed**, 4 new: output cap asserted on the wire, provider body reaching the exception message, and v2/v3 changelog digests.

## Review note

Not self-merging — `main` requires a review, and PRs #29–#31 each merged with 0 reviews recorded, which is worth closing off separately.

items.title: Add ML evaluation harness (precision/recall benchmark for the reviewer)
items.body:
## Evaluation harness — measure the reviewer, don't just trust it

Turns the code reviewer from an unmeasured demo into something with a **report card**: a labeled benchmark + scoring engine that reports precision / recall / F1. This is the ML-engineering foundation for comparing models, prompts, and (later) retrieval.

### What's here (`evals/`)
- **`dataset.py`** — a labeled benchmark: small code files with **known planted bugs** (the answer key / ground truth) across `security`, `correctness`, and `error-handling`, plus **clean** files to catch false positives. Each bug is located by a unique substring, so line numbers are derived from the code and can't drift.
- **`harness.py`** — the scoring engine: builds diffs, runs a reviewer, grades its findings against the answer key into **TP / FP / FN**, and computes **precision / recall / F1**. Also includes a rule-based **baseline** reviewer (no ML) as a yardstick.
- **`run_eval.py`** — CLI that prints the report card. Runs the baseline with no API key, or the real LLM reviewer with `OPENAI_API_KEY`.
- **`README.md`** — how it works + the metrics.

### Metrics
- **Precision** = TP / (TP + FP) — of what it flagged, how much was a real bug.
- **Recall** = TP / (TP + FN) — of the real bugs, how many it caught.

Matching is line-based with a small tolerance; a stronger version would use an **LLM-as-judge** to match by meaning.

### Baseline result (the yardstick)
```
Precision: 100%   Recall: 60%   F1: 75%
```
The regex baseline catches syntactic issues (weak hash, hardcoded secret, SQL injection, `eval`, bare `except`, resource leak) but **misses every semantic/correctness bug** (index error, division-by-zero, off-by-one, mutable default) — because rules can't reason about what the code *does*, and it produces zero false positives on the clean files. That gap is exactly what the LLM reviewer should close; `--reviewer llm` measures whether it does.

### How to run
```bash
python evals/run_eval.py --reviewer baseline          # no key needed
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... python evals/run_eval.py --reviewer llm
```

### Roadmap this unlocks
With a measuring stick in place: compare GPT-4o vs mini, A/B prompts, then add **RAG** and measure the recall gain, then an **agentic/self-verifying** pass and measure the precision gain.

items.title: Detect reordered critical steps as HIGH regression; match findings on semantic identity
items.body:
## What & why

The adversarial robustness corpus scored **F1 0.769 (3/5)** in *both* Python and Swift. Investigation (including running the Swift CLI to confirm identical scores) showed **neither failure was an engine-accuracy bug** — both were ground-truth/harness issues, one of which also revealed a real, fixable capability gap.

### Fix 1 — match findings on semantic identity, not reasoning prose
**Partial Trace Truncation** was scored as `FP=1, FN=1` even though the engine emitted exactly the right findings. Cause: benchmark scoring compared findings by full structural equality, *including the human-facing `reasoning` string*, while the ground truth left it blank. A correct detection became a simultaneous false-positive + false-negative. `_match_key` now erases the free-text `reasoning` before matching; `level` and `strength` stay significant.

### Fix 2 — reordered CRITICAL step → HIGH regression (the "limitation")
**Dependency Inversion Trap** (two dependent critical decisions run in opposite order) produced *no* regression risk. Added the order-analog of the existing "removed critical step → HIGH" rule: a **reordered CRITICAL step is HIGH (strength 1.0)**. It fires only on CRITICAL steps, so benign reordering of structural/diagnostic steps stays `NONE` — the passing standard "Reordered Execution" case (which reorders structural steps) is provably unaffected.

## Contract & verification
- Pinned the new rule into the **frozen Trace Spec v1 conformance vectors** (`alignment_verdict` case 4) — reproduced by the **Swift `ConformanceHarness`** (`ALL VECTORS REPRODUCED ✓`).
- Corrected the adversarial ground-truth labels (blank → accurate reasoning strings).
- Updated `TRACE_SPEC_v1.md §10.2` + `README.md`.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Benchmark (both corpora) | **13/13**, P/R/F1 **1.000** |
| Test suite | **168 passed**, 2 skipped |
| Conformance | **28 cases** pass |
| Swift parity | engine + matcher mirrored; benchmark 13/13; conformance harness reproduces new vector |

## Caveat (intentional)
This is critical-**order** sensitivity, not true dependency-graph inference. It catches dependency inversion because the swapped steps are critical, but would also flag reordering of two genuinely-independent critical steps (loosen via `max_regression_level`). True dependency inference remains scoped future work.

> The matching Swift engine/harness changes are landing separately in the DProvenanceKit (Swift) repo.
