items.title: feat(analyst): trace analysts run official DSPy RLMs; retire the Ax stack
items.body:
## What

Trace analysts are now recursive research programs: the official `dspy.RLM` runs in a sandboxed Deno/Pyodide child process with seven allowlisted trace tools, strict JSON I/O, and metered model calls through the external-optimizer proxy. `callLlmJson` survives only as the explicit one-shot `direct` benchmark baseline. The Ax stack (`ax-service`, `ax-cost-service`, `trace-analyst/loop`, `AxGepaSteeringOptimizer`, the `@ax-llm/ax` dependency) is deleted — audited zero external callers.

New engine boundary: `src/analyst/engine.ts`, `dspy-rlm-engine.ts`, `trace-tool-callback.ts`, `benchmark-public-rlm.ts`, and `clients/python/src/agent_eval_rpc/dspy_rlm_bridge.py` (official `dspy.RLM` in a child process; 14 dedicated tests plus a live-Deno inspect path).

## Why

The published CodeTraceBench numbers (13.47% all-row / 32.73% scored F1 with test artifacts; 15.02% / 30.99% trajectory-only) came from the one-shot direct runner. The recursive-RLM engine is the path to beating that; the semantics were pinned as "a trace analyst IS an RLM program", and the code now matches.

## Audit hardening (two independent adversarial passes)

Security/correctness and API/DX audits ran against the full range. Fixed in this PR:

- **Fabricated-evidence hole (HIGH):** excerpt verification recursed over every string field of a span, so an excerpt matching a `span_id`, status, name, or a timestamp digit verified. Excerpts now match span `attributes`/`status_message` (or a cited finding's content fields) only, with an 8-char minimum; six attack cases pinned as tests.
- **Unpinned sandbox runtime (HIGH):** DSPy's `runner.js` imports `npm:pyodide` unversioned and `--no-config` means no lockfile — npm `latest` flipped `0.29.3` → `314.0.3` during development, silently switching interpreters. An import map now pins `pyodide@314.0.3` and the pin is recorded in runtime identity.
- **Hardcoded attestation (HIGH):** `_runtime_identity` ignored the deno command and reported constants. The sandbox record is now derived from the command that ran (config, node-modules-dir, permission flags with scoped-path counts, never raw paths).
- **All-or-nothing finding parse (MED):** one malformed row from the bridge discarded the whole paid investigation; rows now validate per row with logged rejections counted in `runtime.rejectedFindings`.
- **Bridge/schema contradiction (MED):** the bridge's canonical fixture certified subject `step:2`, which the TypeScript finding-subject grammar rejects; fixture now emits `incorrect-step-2`.
- **Whitespace abort (MED):** a trailing newline on `answer`/`findings_json` raised after all money was spent; model output is stripped before validation.
- **Red release gate (BLOCKER):** `verify-package-exports` demanded the deleted `buildTraceAnalystTools`; it now negative-pins all removed exports. CHANGELOG documents the full breaking surface. The benchmark README states its numbers describe the retired runner and forbids citing them for the new engine without a fresh certified run.

What the security audit could NOT break: live sandbox escape attempts (host FS, network, env, subprocess — all blocked), tool-allowlist bypass (enforced on both sides, zero schema drift across all 7 tools), secret leakage into the child (allowlisted env, ephemeral proxy token only), ReDoS (RE2JS), subprocess leaks (process-group kill with escalation), and the store-backed citation check (base64/foreign ids rejected; net-new versus the pre-image).

## Known deferred (audit findings not in this PR)

- No real-seam integration test in CI: Python tests mock dspy, TS tests mock the bridge. The cheap token-free version (real tool specs through the real bridge validator + a real interpreter boot) is the highest-value follow-up.
- Reasoning models can report `output_tokens` above the completion cap; the proxy's over-output rejection then kills the run (availability, not cost, is the exposure).
- Tool-budget exhaustion surfaces as a bare HTTP 429 to the RLM (`maxToolCalls` not forwarded; response body dropped by `raise_for_status`), burning iterations.
- `--max-cost-usd` feeds both the per-analysis and run-wide caps; per-analysis needs its own flag.
- The implementation digest discovers TypeScript via the import graph but hardcodes the two Python files.
- `traced-analyst` step spans are emitted post-hoc with ~0 duration (`onTurn` removal).
- Missing-Python DX is a raw `ModuleNotFoundError`; the bridge's `inspect` preflight exists but is unwired from TypeScript.
- Legacy "kind" vocabulary remains on constants (`DEFAULT_TRACE_ANALYST_KINDS`, `*_KIND_SPEC`, `kind-factory.ts`).

## Verification

- TypeScript: `pnpm typecheck` clean; `pnpm test` 4,525 passed / 0 failed / 3 skipped (339 files); `pnpm build` + `node scripts/verify-package-exports.mjs` green.
- Python: 17/17 bridge tests; live `inspect` through real Deno booting pinned pyodide `314.0.3` with the derived attestation. (`test_official_optimizer_compatibility`/skillopt failures in a local venv reproduce identically at the merge base — environment extras, not this change.)
- Benchmark digests: implementation `44633a52…` (78 files), dependency lock `b00ffeed…` (4 files), checker green.

## Not in this PR

A fresh certified benchmark run with the DSPy engine (paid) and the labeled comparison against the retired runner's numbers. Until that lands, no headline accuracy number may be cited for the new engine — the reference-result test and benchmark README both enforce the provenance split.

| category | count | mean F1 |

| 4 (open-domain) | 148 | 0.569 |
| 5 (adversarial) | 3 | 0.667 |

Retrieval evidence coverage: **63.4%** (1019/1607 annotated evidence dialog IDs present in top-10 hybrid search hits) — computed across the **full 10-conversation dataset** (all conversations were ingested for this run, so this coverage number is now dataset-wide, not subset-limited).

**Wall-clock: 67.0 minutes** end-to-end (21.8 min ingestion + 43.2 min answer generation, avg 3.09s/QA-pair), **$0 cost** (pre-provisioned API key, no per-token billing in this harness's accounting), **zero rate-limit/retry/hard-stop events** across all 840 calls.

### Subset selection method (non-cherry-picked, same discipline as the prior run)

A real-context sizing sample (16 QA pairs, 2 conversations, real retrieved excerpts) measured ~4.2s/QA-pair for `ollama-cloud` vs. local Ollama's ~60s/QA-pair — roughly 14x faster. Projecting the **full** 1,986-pair dataset from that rate: ~140 min answering + ~21 min ingestion ≈ **2.6 hours** — still over a 90-minute target. So: **all 10 conversations were ingested** (`LUNA_LOCOMO_SAMPLE_LIMIT=10`, giving full-dataset retrieval coverage), and **the first 84 QA pairs of each conversation were scored** (`LUNA_LOCOMO_QA_LIMIT=84` — every conversation has ≥105 QA pairs, so this is a uniform cap, not cherry-picked), for 840 QA pairs total. `LUNA_LOCOMO_MAX_MINUTES=85` was set as an adaptive safety backstop; it never triggered — the run finished cleanly on its own at 67.0 minutes.

## Prior result — local `llama3.1:8b` via Ollama (secondary comparison point)

Kept here because it's an interesting model-quality delta on the **exact same retrieval pipeline** — same ingestion, same hybrid search, same F1 scoring, only the answer-generation model changes.

**Overall F1: 0.352** (32 QA pairs — first 8 QA pairs of the first 4 conversations, `conv-26`/`conv-30`/`conv-41`/`conv-42`, non-cherry-picked)

| category | count | mean F1 |
|:---|---:|---:|
| 1 (multi-hop) | 11 | 0.527 |
| 2 (single-hop) | 16 | 0.272 |
| 3 (temporal) | 3 | 0.111 |
| 4 (open-domain) | 2 | 0.386 |
| 5 (adversarial) | 0 | — (none landed in this small subset) |

Retrieval evidence coverage (same 4-conversation subset): 61.1% (33/54). Wall-clock: 31.3 minutes for 32 QA pairs (~60s/QA-pair, CPU-bound). At that rate the full dataset would have taken ~33 hours — this is the reason the cloud backend was added.

**Reading the two side by side**: retrieval evidence coverage is close (61.1% vs. 63.4%, and the cloud run's number is over 5x more QA pairs / the full dataset, so it's the more trustworthy figure) — the bulk of the F1 gap (0.352 → 0.488) comes from `gpt-oss:120b` extracting answers from the same retrieved context more accurately than `llama3.1:8b`, not from better retrieval. That's expected: answer-from-context quality and retrieval quality are separate things this harness deliberately isolates (see "What's measured vs. not" below).

## What model answered — three backends now available

- **`ollama-cloud`** (current recommendation) — Ollama's hosted cloud API, `https://ollama.com/api/chat`, same request/response shape as local Ollama, Bearer-authenticated via a pre-provisioned key (resolved from a secret manager at run time only, never logged/committed). Default model `gpt-oss:120b` (`LUNA_LOCOMO_CLOUD_MODEL` to override). 429/5xx/network errors retry with short exponential backoff; a HARD failure (bad auth, a quota/billing signal, or throttling that never clears after retries) throws `LocomoHardStopError`, caught specifically in `run.ts` to stop the entire run immediately and write partial results — this prevents a broken key or exhausted quota from silently burning through the rest of a large run one failed retry-loop at a time. None of that triggered during this run (zero errors of any kind across 840 calls).
- **`ollama`** (local, harness default when `LUNA_LOCOMO_ANSWER_BACKEND` is unset) — `llama3.1:8b` via a local Ollama daemon, unchanged from the prior PR revision. No API key, no dollar cost, but ~14x slower per QA pair than the cloud backend on this hardware.
- **`anthropic`** — unchanged, still blocked (no real `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in this environment).

Since LoCoMo scoring is pure token-overlap F1 (no LLM judge — see `scoring.ts`), swapping the answer backend only affects answer quality and wall-clock time, never scoring cost.

## Dataset / license caveat (unchanged)

Dataset: `snap-research/locomo`, `data/locomo10.json` (ACL 2024 paper, arXiv:2402.17753). **License: CC BY-NC 4.0 (NonCommercial)** — this is internal R&D benchmarking of Luna's own retrieval, not redistribution or commercial exploitation. The dataset is **never committed to this repo** — `dataset.ts` downloads it into a git-ignored `.cache/` directory on first run. See `packages/memory/src/adapters/locomo-eval/README.md` "Dataset & license" for the full discussion — anyone wanting to surface this number externally (marketing, blog post, comparison table) should get separate legal sign-off first.

## What's measured vs. not (unchanged)

Luna's memory system (`packages/memory`) is **pure retrieval** — no ingest-time reasoning/synthesis, unlike Honcho (Plastic Labs), which derives facts/resolves contradictions/builds a "theory of mind" of each peer at write time. This harness ingests raw LoCoMo dialog turns only (not the paper's own pre-computed summaries), retrieves via the exact `MemoryRouter.search()` path `memory_search` uses, and answers using ONLY the retrieved excerpt texts — no full transcript, no ground truth in the prompt. So: this measures **Luna's retrieval quality + answer-from-context quality**, not Honcho-equivalent ingest-time synthesis. Also not measured: exact Porter-stemmed F1 (lightweight suffix-stripping approximation instead — internally consistent across our own runs, not bit-for-bit comparable to the published LoCoMo leaderboard numbers).

## A bug found and fixed along the way

While sizing the `ollama-cloud` run, the existing wall-clock projection guard (`LUNA_LOCOMO_MAX_MINUTES`) fired and stopped the run after ingesting a single conversation, before a single answer call had completed. Root cause: the guard's pre-first-call fallback estimate (60s/QA-pair) was calibrated for local `llama3.1:8b` and got reused for `ollama-cloud` too — multiplied across 840 planned QA pairs, that wrong guess alone projected 855 minutes before any real measurement existed. Fixed with (1) a per-backend fallback constant (`ollama-cloud`: 10s, a conservative 2x bound over the ~4.2s measured average) and (2) not enforcing the cap at all until 5 real answer calls have completed, so the projection uses measured data instead of a guess. Also added a 60-second per-attempt request timeout to the new cloud path (previously unbounded — a hang would have blocked the harness indefinitely). Re-verified all 17 unit tests + a typecheck pass before re-running.

## What to survey

Try re-running the sizing/smoke path yourself, resolving `OLLAMA_CLOUD_KEY` from your own secret manager first (see `packages/memory/src/adapters/locomo-eval/README.md` for the harness's secret-handling notes):

```sh
OLLAMA_CLOUD_KEY="$(resolve-your-secret ollama-cloud-key)"   # your own retrieval command
LUNA_EMBEDDER=ollama LUNA_LOCOMO_ANSWER_BACKEND=ollama-cloud \
  LUNA_LOCOMO_SAMPLE_LIMIT=1 LUNA_LOCOMO_QA_LIMIT=5 \
  OLLAMA_CLOUD_KEY="$OLLAMA_CLOUD_KEY" \
  bun packages/memory/src/adapters/locomo-eval/run.ts
```

Expect it to complete in well under a minute of answer-generation time (ingestion of 1 conversation still takes ~90s), with coherent, context-grounded answers. The number that matters most for judging Luna's own retrieval (as opposed to any particular model's answer-extraction skill) is the **63.4% evidence coverage** figure — now computed across the full 10-conversation dataset rather than a 4-conversation slice. The **0.488 overall F1** is the headline "how good is Luna's memory pipeline end-to-end" number going forward; the 0.352 local-llama figure is kept as a secondary reference point for the answer-model quality delta, not as the primary result anymore.

---

## LLM-judge re-scoring — a number comparable to vendor benchmarks

F1 (above) is LoCoMo's own paper metric, but it is **not** what memory-product
vendors report as their headline LoCoMo number — they report **LLM-judge
binary accuracy** (a judge model looks at the question, gold answer, and
prediction, and scores 1/correct or 0/incorrect). F1 and judge-accuracy are
different metrics and are not directly comparable — F1 punishes a
correct-but-differently-phrased answer, so a raw "our 48.8 F1 vs. their 89.9%"
comparison would be misleading in both directions.

`judge-rescore.ts` (new in this update) re-scores the SAME 840 predictions
from the F1 run above with an independently-written LLM judge — zero
re-ingestion, re-retrieval, or re-answering, purely a re-scoring pass over
data already on disk. See `packages/memory/src/adapters/locomo-eval/README.md`
"LLM-judge re-scoring" for the full methodology (judge prompt, category-5
handling, concurrency/retry discipline).

**Overall judge accuracy: 52.6%** (442/840), judge model `gpt-oss:120b`
(same backbone as the answer model, for a same-model comparison), 7.1
minutes wall-clock, 837 judge calls, **zero parse failures, zero
rate-limit/hard-stop events**.

| category | count | judge accuracy | F1 (same predictions) |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 (multi-hop) | 277 | 0.368 | 0.397 |
| 2 (single-hop) | 319 | 0.602 | 0.585 |
| 3 (temporal) | 93 | 0.387 | 0.289 |
| 4 (open-domain) | 148 | 0.743 | 0.569 |
| 5 (adversarial) | 3 | 0.667 | 0.667 (identical by construction — see README) |
| **OVERALL** | **840** | **0.526** | **0.488** |

**Sanity checks that this is a real metric difference, not a scoring bug**:
per-category rank correlation between F1 and judge-accuracy is Spearman
ρ = 0.600 (tracks — same rough category ordering, most divergence is
explained below); mean F1 is 0.724 for QA pairs the judge calls correct vs.
0.225 for ones it calls incorrect (strong separation — the two metrics
agree on most individual QA pairs even where the category-level numbers
diverge). Where they diverge most (cat1 judge lower than F1, cat3/cat4
judge notably higher than F1) has a specific, checkable explanation, not a
bug: F1 gives cat1 (multi-hop) partial credit per comma-joined sub-answer
even when the full compound answer isn't entirely right, while the binary
judge only credits a fully correct compound answer; F1 punishes cat3/cat4
answers for phrasing/format differences ("7th of May, 2023" vs "7 May
2023") that the judge correctly treats as equivalent.

## Comparison to vendor-reported LoCoMo numbers

| System | LoCoMo score | Metric | Dataset coverage |
|:---|---:|:---|:---|
| **Luna (this PR)** | **52.6%** | LLM-judge accuracy, our own judge prompt, `gpt-oss:120b` judge | 840/1,986 pairs (42.3%), non-cherry-picked (first 84 QA pairs × 10 conversations) |
| Honcho (Plastic Labs) | 89.9% | LLM-judge accuracy (self-reported) | Unknown, likely full dataset |
| Hindsight | up to 89.6% (Gemini-3 backbone), 83.6% cited elsewhere | LLM-judge accuracy (self-reported) | Unknown |
| ByteRover 2.0 | 92.2% | LLM-judge accuracy (self-reported) | Unknown, likely full dataset |

**Read this table with real caveats, not as a leaderboard**:

- These are **self-reported vendor numbers**, most likely on the **full
  1,986-pair dataset**; ours is **840/1,986 (42.3%)** — the same
  non-cherry-picked subset the F1 number above was computed on (see "Subset
  selection method" above for why: full-dataset wall-clock was ~2.6h,
  outside this session's budget).
- **Different judge models.** We don't know exactly what judge model each
  vendor used. Ours is our own independently-written prompt (not copied
  from any vendor's, which aren't published) against `gpt-oss:120b`. Judge
  choice can itself shift the score by a meaningful margin.
- **Different answer/backbone models.** We don't know each vendor's
  backbone; ours is `gpt-oss:120b` throughout (embeddings via local Ollama,
  answer generation and judge both via Ollama Cloud).
- **Architecturally different systems, not just a quality gap.** Honcho
  explicitly does ingest-time reasoning/synthesis (deriving facts,
  resolving contradictions, building a "theory of mind" of each peer).
  Luna's memory is **pure retrieval** — `memory_save` stores exactly what
  it's given, no synthesis step. Some of this gap is very likely
  architectural, not a quality bug in Luna's retrieval — see
  "Recommendations" below for what the failure-mode data says about how
  much of it is retrieval-tunable vs. not.

## Retrieval-vs-judge failure-mode breakdown

Cross-referencing each QA pair's retrieval-evidence coverage (was the FULL
set of LoCoMo's annotated gold-evidence dialog turns present in the top-10
hybrid-search hits?) against judge correctness splits every failure into a
RETRIEVAL problem (evidence never surfaced) or a MODEL problem (evidence
surfaced, extraction/reasoning still wrong):

**Overall (836 QA pairs with annotated evidence; 4 category-3 pairs have no
annotated evidence in the dataset itself and are excluded)**:

| | Judge correct | Judge incorrect |
|:---|---:|---:|
| Evidence found (all gold turns in top-10) | 365 (68.6% of found) | 167 |
| Evidence missing (partial or none) | 75 (24.7% of missing) | 229 |

Evidence was found for 532/836 (63.6%) — matches the F1 run's independently
computed retrieval-coverage figure (63.4%) almost exactly, a good
cross-check that both passes are looking at the same retrieval reality. **Of
all 396 incorrect answers: 57.8% are retrieval failures (evidence missing),
42.2% are model failures (evidence found but still wrong)** — roughly
balanced, with a lean toward retrieval.

**That balance is NOT uniform across categories** — this is the part worth
acting on:

| category | evidence-found rate | of failures: retrieval-attributable | of failures: model-attributable |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 (multi-hop) | 36.1% (**lowest**) | **78.3%** | 21.7% |
| 2 (single-hop) | 82.8% | 31.5% | **68.5%** (**highest**) |
| 3 (temporal) | 47.2% | 63.6% | 36.4% |
| 4 (open-domain) | 83.8% (**highest**) | 42.1% | 57.9% |

- **Category 1 (multi-hop, 277/840 = the largest category) is overwhelmingly
  a retrieval problem.** Its evidence-found rate (36.1%) is by far the
  lowest of any category, and 78.3% of its failures are evidence-missing.
  Multi-hop ground truth is comma-joined sub-answers needing multiple
  distinct evidence turns; a single hybrid-search call over the whole
  question likely under-retrieves for multi-part questions.
- **Category 2 (single-hop, 319/840 = the second-largest category) is
  overwhelmingly a model problem.** Evidence is found 82.8% of the time
  (second-highest), yet 68.5% of its failures happen anyway with the right
  memory already retrieved — the highest model-attributable failure share
  of any category with a meaningful sample size.
- **Category 3 (temporal) — this corrects an unverified claim in the
  original F1-run write-up.** The prior revision of this PR's README
  speculated (from F1 scores alone, no evidence-coverage cross-check) that
  cat3's low score was "mostly relative-date phrasing, not a retrieval
  miss." The judge-rescore data does not support that as the primary
  driver: **63.6% of cat3's failures are evidence-missing** (retrieval,
  the larger share), and cat3's evidence-found rate (47.2%) is well below
  cat2/cat4. There IS a real secondary reasoning signal, though — even when
  evidence is found, cat3 is wrong 47.6% of the time (20/42), notably above
  the 31.4% found-but-wrong baseline across all categories — so both
  things are true: retrieval is the bigger lever, but a real temporal-
  reasoning weakness sits on top of it.
- **Category 4 (open-domain) is the healthiest category** — highest
  evidence-found rate (83.8%) and highest judge accuracy (74.3%). Both
  retrieval and answer-extraction are working well here; lowest priority
  for further investigation.

## Recommendations (grounded in the breakdown above, tracked in `workspace.db`)

Each of these is filed as its own row in the `tasks` table (component
`memory`, notes referencing this PR) — not just prose that dies in a PR
description:

1. **[high] Multi-hop (cat 1) retrieval fix — query decomposition or
   targeted topK increase.** Cat1 is the largest category (277/840) with
   the lowest evidence-found rate (36.1%) and 78.3% retrieval-attributable
   failures. Decomposing multi-hop questions into per-clause sub-queries
   (or raising topK specifically for detected multi-part questions) before
   falling back to single-shot hybrid search is the highest-leverage single
   change here — closing cat1's evidence-found rate to cat2's level alone
   projects overall judge accuracy from 52.6% to roughly 60.3%, in
   isolation.
2. **[high] Surface the session date explicitly in the answer prompt for
   temporal questions.** Cat3's evidence-found-but-still-wrong rate (47.6%)
   is well above the 31.4% baseline even though the session date is
   already embedded in every ingested turn's content
   (`[<sessionDateTime>] speaker: text` — see `ingest.ts`). The
   answer-generation prompt (`answer-model.ts`'s `buildPrompt`) never
   instructs the model to resolve relative-date language ("last month",
   "next Friday") against it. Near-zero-cost prompt change, directly
   testable via a before/after judge-rescore pass.
3. **[normal] topK / hybrid-weight tuning specifically for temporal (cat 3)
   retrieval.** Retrieval-missing is cat3's larger failure driver (63.6%),
   not phrasing — see the correction above. Re-run with topK raised (or a
   BM25/vector weight rebalance) for temporal-tagged questions and
   re-measure evidence-found rate via `judge-rescore.ts` before assuming a
   prompt fix alone (recommendation 2) is sufficient.
4. **[normal] Stronger answer-extraction prompting or model for category 2
   (single-hop).** Cat2 (319/840, the second-largest category) already has
   strong retrieval (82.8% evidence-found) but 68.5% of its failures happen
   anyway — the highest model-attributable share of any sizable category.
   Further retrieval tuning has limited remaining room here; the lever is
   prompting (e.g. instruct the model to quote the exact matching phrase
   before answering) or a model with stronger extraction/instruction-
   following than `gpt-oss:120b`.
5. **[low, longer-horizon] Scoped ingest-time synthesis experiment, to test
   how much of the vendor gap is even reachable by retrieval tuning alone.**
   Even a full fix of the single biggest retrieval gap (recommendation 1)
   only projects to ~60% overall — still roughly 30 points short of
   Honcho/Hindsight/ByteRover's 83.6–92.2%. That suggests retrieval tuning
   alone won't close the full gap. Recommend a scoped experiment: ingest
   LoCoMo's own `session_summary` field (currently deliberately excluded —
   see README "What this measures", since Luna's memory has no ingest-time
   synthesis step) as an ADDITIONAL retrievable record type alongside raw
   turns, and re-measure cat1 (multi-hop) evidence-found rate via
   `judge-rescore.ts`. This tests the synthesis-vs-retrieval-tuning
   tradeoff with data instead of assuming an architecture change is
   required.

## What to survey (this update)

Try `bun packages/memory/src/adapters/locomo-eval/judge-rescore.ts`
against the existing `.out/results-*.json` (resolve `OLLAMA_CLOUD_KEY` the
same way as the answer-generation step — see the README's secret-handling
notes). Expect it to complete in ~7 minutes for the full 840-pair set, print
the per-category judge-accuracy table + the retrieval-vs-judge 2x2 above,
and write `.out/judge-<stamp>.json`. The single most load-bearing number to
sanity-check yourself: **63.6% evidence-found rate**, computed two
independent ways (the original F1 run's retrieval-coverage pass and this
judge-rescore's crosstab) and landing within 0.2 points of each other —
that agreement is what makes the retrieval-vs-model failure split above
trustworthy rather than a one-off artifact.



---

## Retrieval-fix experiment: diagnosis, implementation, and a real (mixed) result

Following the recommendations above, this update diagnoses category 1's
retrieval gap empirically (rather than assuming a fix), implements three
gated retrieval-mode options plus a deterministic temporal-date index, and
runs a real before/after comparison. The retrieval-only numbers were
gathered by a dev-agent working in a separate sandboxed session; that
session had no GitHub credentials or Ollama Cloud key available to it, so
I (Jax) pushed its commit and ran the live answer+judge comparison myself
in a follow-up turn.

### Diagnosis (empirical, category 1 / multi-hop)

Re-ran retrieval at topK up to 100 for category-1 QA pairs across two
conversations (202 evidence dialog IDs checked). **68% of evidence missing
from a top-10 result set was already present in the same ranked candidate
list, just below rank 10** — a result-COUNT budget problem, not an
embedding-quality problem. 96% of category-1 evidence spans multiple
sessions, so a single flat top-10 has to split its budget across several
sub-topics at once. The remaining 32% never surfaced even at rank ≤100 (a
smaller, genuinely-not-retrieved component).

### What was implemented (all gated, default behavior unchanged)

- `LUNA_LOCOMO_RETRIEVAL_MODE=flat` (default) `| decompose | hierarchical`:
  - **flat @ higher `LUNA_LOCOMO_TOPK`** — the direct fix for the dominant
    cause above; no new retrieval logic, just raising an existing knob.
  - **`decompose`** — splits literally-conjunctive multi-hop questions into
    sub-queries, merges/dedupes results. Honest negative-ish finding: only
    ~9.6% of this dataset's category-1 questions are literally splittable;
    on the tested sample it was a no-op, identical to flat.
  - **`hierarchical`** — deterministic (no-LLM) per-session lexical
    summaries, ranks sessions by term-overlap, boosts hits from
    top-ranked sessions in a widened candidate pool. An uncapped first
    version *regressed* retrieval (33.0% vs. 58.5% flat baseline on the
    same QA pairs) — a mis-ranked priority session crowded out
    well-scored hits. Capping the boost at half of topK improved it to
    50.0%, still below the flat baseline. **Stays off by default** — the
    session-relevance signal needs to be better before this is worth
    adopting. This was the PageIndex-style hierarchical-navigation idea;
    it didn't pan out in its first form, documented honestly rather than
    hidden.
- `LUNA_LOCOMO_DATE_INDEX=1` (default off) — injects a deterministic,
  zero-LLM-call "Session dates for reference" block into the answer
  prompt, so the model can resolve relative-date language against real
  dates instead of guessing.

16 new unit tests for the pure logic (`decomposeQuestion`, `mergeHits`,
`buildSessionSummaries`, `rankSessions`, `prioritizeBySessions`), all
passing (42 total in the suite).

### Live comparison — flat@topK=30 + date-index vs. flat@topK=10 baseline

Run on a 95-QA-pair subset (3 conversations — `conv-26`, `conv-30`,
`conv-41` — categories 1 and 3 only, `gpt-oss:120b` via Ollama Cloud, same
methodology as the full run above), single run each (no repeat — flagged
explicitly per the caveat below):

| | Evidence coverage | F1 (cat 1) | F1 (cat 3) | F1 (overall) | Judge acc. (cat 1) | Judge acc. (cat 3) | Judge acc. (overall) |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Baseline** (topK=10, no date index) | 61.2% | 0.472 | 0.325 | 0.440 | 45.9% | 38.1% | **44.2%** |
| **Fix** (topK=30 + date index) | **80.8%** | 0.517 | 0.290 | 0.467 | 47.3% | 28.6% | **43.2%** |

**This is not a clean win, and I'm reporting it as such rather than
spinning it.** Evidence coverage jumped 20 points (61.2% → 80.8%,
confirming the diagnosis was right), and F1 moved up slightly
(0.440 → 0.467). But **judge accuracy barely moved and went slightly
DOWN overall** (44.2% → 43.2%) — category 1 improved marginally
(45.9% → 47.3%) but category 3 got notably worse (38.1% → 28.6%).

Two things temper how much to read into this:

1. **Two variables changed at once** (topK AND date-index together), so
   the category-3 regression can't be cleanly attributed to either one.
   It's plausible the date-index text is adding noise/confusion for
   temporal questions specifically, or that widening topK to 30 pulls in
   more distracting excerpts even when the right evidence is already
   present, or it's simply noise.
2. **Category 3 has only 21 QA pairs in this subset.** A couple of
   flipped answers swings the percentage by ~10 points. Per the
   engram-kit lesson already folded into this PR (a single-run delta
   under ~2 points isn't trustworthy without repeated runs), this result
   should be read as **inconclusive, not as evidence the fix failed or
   succeeded** — more retrieval clearly happened, whether it translates to
   more correct answers needs a cleaner, larger, and/or repeated
   experiment before concluding either way.

**What this means going forward:** the recommendation isn't "ship
topK=30 as the new default." It's "retrieval coverage and answer
correctness are not the same thing, confirmed with data, not assumed" —
exactly the gap the retrieval-vs-judge failure breakdown above predicted
(evidence-found-but-still-wrong is a real, separate failure mode from
evidence-missing). Next step, if pursued: isolate topK-only and
date-index-only as separate single-variable experiments, and run each at
least twice before trusting the direction of any delta under ~2-3 points.

### What to survey (this update)

All three retrieval modes and the date index are env-gated and off/flat
by default — the original 840-pair headline numbers above are unaffected.
To reproduce the live comparison: run
`packages/memory/src/adapters/locomo-eval/run.ts` twice with
`LUNA_LOCOMO_CATEGORY_FILTER=1,3 LUNA_LOCOMO_SAMPLE_LIMIT=3`, once at
`LUNA_LOCOMO_TOPK=10` and once at `LUNA_LOCOMO_TOPK=30
LUNA_LOCOMO_DATE_INDEX=1`, then `judge-rescore.ts` against each results
file.

items.title: fix: repair CHANGELOG rolling + add offline (Ubuntu) LLM training code
items.body: ## 1. Fix: CHANGELOG wasn't recording release notes **Root cause:** `scripts/build_release.py`'s `UNRELEASED_HEADER_RE` only matched a *dated* header `[unreleased] - `, but the file uses a **bare** `[unreleased]`. So the roller never found the section: real notes piled up under a never‑rolled `[unreleased]`, while the bot appended a cascade of empty `[0.2.x] - release build (no itemized changes)` sections. **Fix:** - Regex now matches both bare and dated headers (`^\[unreleased\]\s*(?:-.*)?$`). - Repaired `CHANGELOG.txt`: collapsed the broken empty cascade and consolidated all the orphaned notes into a real **`[0.3.0]`** section; fresh `[unreleased]` on top. Set `VERSION=0.3.0` and synced the web version. - Added `scripts/tests/test_build_release.py` (regression test) and wired `scripts/tests` into CI/Makefile. Going forward the bot rolls `[unreleased]` → `[X.Y.Z]` correctly (verified: `--check` now finds the items; tests cover bare + dated headers + minor‑bump threshold). ## 2. Offline (Linux/Ubuntu) LLM training code You can now run training offline on your own box: - `training/export.py` — class sessions/feedback → JSONL (dependency‑free; fairness guardrail enforced — no `race`/`ethnicity` in conditioning). - `training/run_finetune.py` — QLoRA on CUDA (4‑bit via bitsandbytes), LoRA/CPU fallback otherwise; fully offline (`HF_HUB_OFFLINE`/`TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE`, local base‑model path). items.title: D1: real per-question snapshots — MMLU (+DROP) from the Open LLM Leaderboard archive
items.body:
## What changed & why

This PR bundles two **real evaluation datasets** as CSV snapshots, giving the demo genuine per-question data instead of illustrative numbers. For two well-known open models — **meta-llama/Llama-2-70b-hf** and **tiiuae/falcon-40b** — we snapshot per-question correctness logs from the Open LLM Leaderboard v1 archive on HuggingFace (the leaderboard's public "details" datasets, produced by the EleutherAI evaluation harness):

- **`datasets/mmlu.csv`** — MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding), 14,042 questions per model, each scored 0/1, grouped into **57 subject clusters** (`cluster_id` = subject name).
- **`datasets/drop.csv`** — DROP (a reading-comprehension benchmark), 9,536 questions per model, scored with token-F1 in [0,1], grouped into **579 passage clusters** (`cluster_id` = a short SHA-1 prefix of the passage text — questions about the same passage share a cluster).

Both follow the project CSV schema `benchmark,model,item_id,cluster_id,score`, with identical item sets across the two models (asserted by the generator), so paired statistics work out of the box. **Deliberately excluded:** benchmark questions, reference answers, and model outputs — we redistribute *scores and group labels only*, which is all the statistics need and keeps us clear of redistributing benchmark content.

`scripts/fetch_hf_data.py` is the exact, re-runnable script that produced the CSVs (source repos, run timestamps, structural assertions, license note in its docstring); `scripts/README.md` summarizes provenance and regeneration.

Two non-obvious findings worth a reviewer's attention:
1. **DROP absolute scores are low** (mean F1 6.62% vs 6.41%). That is a real property of the archived v1 evaluation — a known harness answer-parsing issue that led HuggingFace to remove DROP from the leaderboard in late 2023. We keep it as-is (documented in `scripts/README.md`) because the per-passage clustering structure, which is what this demo analyzes, is genuine; our extracted means match the archive's own aggregate `results_*.json` to four decimal places.
2. The archive evaluated **one DROP query UUID twice** (same question, both models, same positions); its second occurrence gets a `#2` suffix so item ids stay unique.

Headline numbers: MMLU means 69.19% (Llama-2-70b-hf) vs 55.88% (falcon-40b), n=14,042, 57 clusters (spot-checked per-subject against the archive's own results JSON — exact match). DROP means 6.62% vs 6.41%, n=9,536, 579 clusters. Each CSV is under 2 MB (1.76 MB / 1.33 MB), so no subsampling was needed.

## How this fits the bigger picture

This is part of **Deliverable slice 2** of Fluke — the interactive demo of "Adding Error Bars to Evals" (arXiv:2411.00640). These files power the two "real data" entries in the dataset picker (the mockup's DROP and MMLU cards, currently showing illustrative numbers) and will be parsed by the C branch's CSV parser when the B2 convergence node wires everything together.

## How to verify

Sanity checks run before commit (a short Python pass over both CSVs, shown in the PR discussion below if needed):

- header is exactly `benchmark,model,item_id,cluster_id,score`; scores all within [0,1]; MMLU scores strictly 0/1
- both models present with **identical item_id sets** per benchmark; no duplicate `(model, item_id)` rows; each item's cluster_id consistent across models
- cluster counts: 57 (MMLU) / 579 (DROP); per-model means match the archive's own `results_*.json` aggregates (DROP F1 to 4 decimal places; MMLU spot-checked per subject — exact match)

Regenerate from source: `python3 scripts/fetch_hf_data.py` (needs `pyarrow`; downloads ~140 MB of parquet, cache dir overridable via `FLUKE_HF_CACHE`). The script re-asserts all structural invariants on every run.

**Test-coverage exception (execution guide §4):** this node ships data artifacts plus their generation script; per the plan, the CSVs are validated downstream by the C1 parser test-suite at convergence (B2), and the generator itself enforces the structural assertions above on every run.

## Acceptance criterion

From the `MIKADO.md` D1 row — *"CSVs in repo with cluster labels + real model names; load in app"* / test plan *"validated by C1 parser"*. Met: both CSVs are in `datasets/` with real cluster labels (57 MMLU subjects, 579 DROP passages) and real model names (Llama-2-70b-hf, falcon-40b); they conform to the project CSV schema so the C1 parser can load them in the app at convergence B2, which is where "load in app" is exercised per the plan. The risk-flagged fallback (synthetic data) was **not** needed — real data landed inside the timebox.

items.title: Harden, test, and advance iSpot toward beta
items.body:
## Summary

Takes iSpot from an untested, host-bound scaffold to a portable, hardened, and tested platform, then adds the advanced capabilities from the roadmap and closes the audit findings. Every change is verified by CI on GitHub (unit job for pure/scoring logic; a new integration job that installs the scientific stack and runs the app end-to-end).

Bundled here because the work built on itself as a single line of commits on `claude/inspect-a81cyw`.

## What changed (by theme)

### Correctness fixes
- **Cluster-count estimator** (`cluster_estimation._find_knee`): the old cumulative-drop heuristic assumed a strictly decreasing curve and collapsed the estimate to the smallest K on the (non-monotonic) spatial-coherence-vs-K curve. Replaced with a direction-agnostic max-distance-to-chord elbow finder in a new dependency-light `ispot/knee.py`.
- **Metrics**: `compute_metrics` now computes **NMI** (ARI/NMI/F1), matching the docs.
- **No-GT scoring**: the O(n) spectral consensus was recomputed once per method; it's now computed once per run and passed in.
- **Meta-learning retrain trigger**: replaced an exact `count % 50` check (a batch insert can skip it entirely) with `count - last_trained_count >= 50`.

### Security & robustness (from the audit)
- **Path traversal** in the download endpoint fixed via `validation.safe_child_path` (rejects `../`/absolute escapes; reproduced then covered by tests).
- **CORS**: replaced `allow_origins=["*"]` (invalid with credentials) with an explicit `ISPOT_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` list.
- **Job status** now distinguishes `completed` / `completed_partial` / `failed`; per-method errors surface in `method_summary` and in the SPA (the frontend no longer polls forever on partial jobs).
- **Upload limits**: extension allowlist, streamed size cap (`ISPOT_MAX_UPLOAD_MB`, HTTP 413), and a spot-count cap (`ISPOT_MAX_SPOTS`) enforced before dispatch.
- **Retention**: `ispot/cleanup.py` removes uploaded-but-never-completed jobs older than `ISPOT_JOB_TTL_DAYS` (default 7).
- **Optional API-key auth** (`ISPOT_API_KEY`, `X-API-Key`) gating the mutating endpoints; disabled by default so single-tenant use is unchanged.
- **Plugin sandbox** (`ispot/sandbox.py`, roadmap #6): plugins run in an isolated subprocess with memory/CPU rlimits and a wall-clock timeout via `plugins.run_plugin_sandboxed`. Network isolation is documented as requiring a locked-down container.

### Portability
- Paths derive from the package location with env overrides (`ISPOT_JOBS_DIR`, `ISPOT_SEED_CSV`, dataset dirs, `runner.py` git root); fixed the meta-learning seed-CSV path that pointed at a host-specific `/mnt/results` so the DB now seeds from the shipped `data/unified_results.csv`.
- **Persistent job store** (`ispot/jobstore.py`): job status is written through to SQLite and restored on startup, so a restart/crash no longer loses jobs. `docker-compose.yml` sketches the API + Redis + worker target.

### Advanced capabilities
- **Meta-learning → gradient-boosted trees + calibration** (roadmap #10): `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` auto-selected over Ridge once a method has enough runs, with isotonic calibration of predicted scores. Uses only scikit-learn.
- **Statistical comparison** in the PDF report (PLAN §1.5.3): Wilcoxon signed-rank + Cliff's delta + Holm–Bonferroni, wired into the report which previously had the section but never populated it.
- **Implemented the two README-promised endpoints** that didn't exist: `GET /api/meta-learning/recommend` and `POST /api/plugins/register` (gated by `ISPOT_ENABLE_PLUGIN_REGISTER`), plus `GET /api/plugins`.

### Testing & CI (was: zero tests)
- Unit suites for knee, Hungarian metrics + NMI, no-GT scoring, job status, upload validation + path traversal, statistical comparison, job store, retention, meta-learning (Ridge/GBT/calibration), sandbox (incl. timeout & memory-cap enforcement), and auth.
- **Integration CI job** installs the runnable scientific stack and runs an end-to-end pipeline smoke test (synthetic dataset → preprocess → Leiden/PCA → no-GT composite → cluster estimation → ranking) plus an API boot + endpoint test. This verifies the platform starts and runs a benchmark outside the original dev container.

## Beta readiness

This PR clears the self-hosted single-tenant beta blockers (portability, boots-and-runs verified, hardening) and adds the hosted-beta gates of auth and plugin sandboxing. Still open before a **public hosted** beta, and intentionally out of scope here: packaging/verifying the heavy method backends (torch/TensorFlow/R + model weights) so more than the deps-light methods run on a clean image; moving job **execution** (not just status) onto Celery/Redis workers with concurrency limits; TLS/rate-limiting; and full multi-tenancy. See the README notes and `docker-compose.yml` for the intended direction.

## Verification

Unit + integration CI jobs are green on the head commit. Pure-logic and stdlib modules were additionally exercised locally.

items.title: Integrate ExtractBench extraction benchmark
items.body:
## What

This PR integrates the complete ExtractBench system into this repository, reframing it from a parse-only benchmark into a benchmark for **schema-guided extraction** from enterprise documents. Given a document and a user-defined JSON Schema, a system must return schema-valid JSON with the correct values, every record of each repeated structure, missing fields marked `null` rather than invented, and source evidence for each value. All existing parse capabilities are preserved.

The benchmark covers **370 documents (4,869 pages)** across 8 business domains and 67 document types, each type with its own schema, tagged along five independent difficulty axes (task challenge, perception challenge, table structure, length, business domain).

## Why

Enterprises write a new schema for almost every workflow, so an extraction system cannot be tuned to a fixed template — it has to handle schemas and documents it has never seen. Because agents increasingly act on extracted values before anyone reviews them, one truncated schedule or one invented value becomes a wrong payment or a wrong decision. The benchmark therefore scores completeness and traceability: unified value F1 as the headline metric, plus word- and page-level grounding F1.

## How

The integration lands as a single squashed change so the repository moves atomically from the parse-only baseline to the full extraction benchmark. Recent parse-side changes on `main` that postdate the extraction work (oi_parser, MinerU-Diffusion, Nemotron-Omni, Gemini 3.6 Flash / 3.5 Flash Lite pipelines, Extend Light, `bbox_scale` coordinate-frame config, formatting-rule fixes) were reconciled and transposed into the renamed package so nothing on `main` is lost.

## Changes

- **Package rename**: `parse_bench` -> `extract_bench` across source, tests, tooling, and project metadata; project renamed to `extract-bench`.
- **Extract task type, end to end**: extraction schemas and test-case loading, inference routing, evaluation metrics (value F1 with per-split precision/recall, row-identity scoring for repeated structures, word- and page-level grounding), and cost accounting.
- **Extract providers and pipelines**: LlamaExtract (Agentic, Agentic Plus, Cost-Effective), coding agents (Claude Code, Codex), direct model APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI Responses, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, vLLM open-weight, NuExtract3), and specialized APIs (Reducto, Extend, Datalab, Pulse, Landing AI, Azure Content Understanding, Lift, table-codegen), with citation and grounding support.
- **Analysis and reporting suite**: leaderboard, aggregation, comparison, and detailed per-document HTML reports with grounding bbox visualization, unified metric selectors, failed-document reporting, and static CSS/JS assets.
- **Leaderboard**: `leaderboard.csv` and README tables now report extract metrics (unified value F1 by length split, word/page grounding F1, cost per page).
- **Runtime hardening**: lazy adapter registry, lazily initialized sub-CLIs, dependency shaving, graceful test skips when runner extras are absent, and a CI workflow (ruff + pytest with and without runner extras).
- **Preserved upstream parse work**, transposed into the new layout: oi_parser provider/pipeline/label mapper/layout adapter; MinerU-Diffusion and Nemotron-Omni pipelines; Gemini 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash Lite pipelines; Extend Light pipeline with `extend-ai>=1.16.0`; `bbox_scale` config gated to providers that pin the perceived image frame; `items_to_markdown` delimiter fix and single-span formatting-rule matching, with their regression tests.
- **Housekeeping**: annotator apps and local data directories are no longer tracked.

## Testing

- Full suite with runner extras: **774 passed**.
- Runner-free suite (matches CI's first stage): **687 passed, 20 skipped**, with the graceful-skip convention applied to the transposed coordinate-frame tests.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean; `uv lock` verified consistent with `pyproject.toml` (`uv sync --locked`).
- Verified file-by-file that the diff against the extraction codebase is limited to the transposed upstream parse commits listed above.

## Notes

- The PR is intentionally a single commit; review is best done by area (schemas, metrics, providers, analysis) rather than commit-by-commit.
- Breaking change for downstream consumers: the Python package import path changes from `parse_bench` to `extract_bench`, and `leaderboard.csv` switches to the extract-metric schema.
- New optional environment variables are documented in `.env.example`; no defaults changed for existing parse pipelines beyond the documented `bbox_scale` gating.

items.title: fix(tools): remove two conformance-harness false-negatives
items.body:
## What

Two scoring artifacts in the tool-calling conformance harness were **understating real scores** — neither is a model defect. Found while auditing the `soak-20260626-100115` results.

### Bug A — `oversize-tool-output` demanded a literal phrasing (affects every backend)
The final-answer assertion was `containsAll: ["exceeds maxBytes", "narrower"]`. A behaviourally-perfect answer (e.g. qwen3.5-9b: calls `read_file`, hits the policy, *"…output size (41,203 bytes) exceeds the maximum allowed limit of 32,768 bytes… read a smaller portion"*, no hallucination) **fails** because it paraphrases instead of echoing those exact substrings — **0 passes across all 5 soak models** despite F1=1.0 tool selection.

Fix: add a `containsAny` assertion kind and re-express the oversize final-answer check as a size-acknowledgement OR-set **and** a narrowing OR-set. The `toolResultErrorKind` honesty gate is unchanged, so a hallucinated answer still fails.

### Bug B — a built-in's required tool was hidden from companion scoring (affects llama.cpp / MLX)
The scorer's expected-set recovery — the fallback for transcripts that omit the `requiredTools` prompt field (companion soaks) — only extracts a tool named in the backtick or bare-dispatch form. Scenarios **06** and **07** worded their `read_file` requirement as free prose, so a *correct* `read_file` call was mis-scored as a false positive. Verified against a real llama-Mistral transcript: those cells read F1≈0.81 with `parallel-readme-comparison` wrongly at 0.0.

Fix: name the tool in backticks in both `toolInvoked` messages (Ollama, which writes authoritative `requiredTools`, was unaffected). A new `ScenarioRecoveryTests` case asserts **every** built-in `toolInvoked` assertion exposes its tool to recovery, so this can't reappear when a scenario is added or reworded.

## Not in scope (already fixed, verified during the audit)
- No-tool F1 drag — already handled (`toolSelection: nil`, excluded from the mean).
- llama.cpp TP attribution (F1=0.000) — already fixed by #2043; current scorer scores that transcript F1≈0.81.

## Tests
- `containsAny` pass / fail / missing-values
- oversize accepts the canonical correct paraphrase, still rejects a hallucinated answer
- built-in recovery coverage for all scenarios

## Backend checklist
- [x] Ollama (unaffected by B; A flips `oversize` to pass for competent models)
- [x] llama.cpp / MLX (B fixes understated `read_file` cells — confirmed on a retained transcript; re-measured by the next cross-backend soak)

items.body:
Two doc correctness fixes in response to review thread comments on PR #951.

# Before
mse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, pred))

items.title: docs(examples): eval-optimization loops (classifier macro-F1, prompt exact-match)
items.body:
## What

Two new examples that demonstrate driving an **eval project to a reported metric** — the `experiment` evaluator's home turf — with the trust guards turned on so "optimize until the number passes" is trustworthy instead of gameable.

| Example | Metric | Model under test | Offline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `examples/eval-classifier/` | **macro-F1 ≥ 0.80** | a rule-based sentiment classifier the agent edits | ✅ zero-dep, runs with no model |
| `examples/eval-prompt/` | **exact-match accuracy ≥ 0.90** | a live LLM; the agent optimizes the prompt | ❌ needs an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (LM Studio by default) |

Both ship a self-contained, zero-dependency target you can run directly, plus a heavily-commented `.loop.yaml`. Wired into `examples/README.md` under a new "Optimizing an eval to a metric" section.

## Why it's more than a metric loop

The #1 failure mode of eval-optimization is the agent **gaming the checker** — editing labels, hardcoding gold answers, overfitting. Both examples defend against exactly that:

- **`evaluatorGuard: error`** on the scorer *and* the datasets → the agent's only lever is the model/prompt; touching the checker ends the run as `evaluator-tampered`.
- **held-out split** → the metric is scored on data the agent is told not to train on and never sees the labels of in feedback.
- **`baseline: strict`** (classifier) → proves the eval starts RED, not vacuously green.
- a paired **correctness gate** (classifier) so the loop can't "win" by breaking the module into something that returns junk.

## Verification

- Both specs `loopgen lint` clean.
- **eval-classifier:** stub baseline scores macro-F1 **0.33** (RED), contract test passes on the stub, a plausible lexicon reaches **1.0** on the real held-out set (bar achievable with margin).
- **eval-prompt:** verified end-to-end against a local LM Studio model (`google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-qat`): stub prompt → accuracy **0.0** (RED), engineered prompt → **1.0**. Stub restored.

Note: the full agent loop (which spends driver budget) was not run; targets and lints were verified directly.

items.title: feat(bench): wire deterministic correctness scorers for amabench + longmemeval (#507)
items.body:
Closes #507.

## What landed

Three atomic commits wire deterministic answer-correctness scoring into the AMA-Bench and LongMemEval adapters so all 11 canonical-bench invocations produce a real correctness grade alongside the existing latency / corpus statistics.

1. **`feat(bench): qa_scoring leaf — normalize/EM/SEM/F1`** — new `benchmarks/qa_scoring.py`, pure-stdlib leaf module exposing `normalize_answer`, `score_exact_match`, `score_substring_exact_match`, `score_f1`, and the `score_multi_answer` best-of wrapper. 24 unit tests cover normalization edge cases, all four score functions, and the determinism contract.
2. **`feat(bench/amabench): wire deterministic correctness scorer`** — `amabench_adapter` now scores per-question retrieval against the gold answer, emitting overall `exact_match` / `substring_exact_match` / `f1` plus `accuracy_by_type` and `accuracy_by_domain` breakdowns. Aggregator handles legacy per_question rows missing score fields. 6 unit tests.
3. **`feat(bench/longmemeval): wire deterministic correctness scorer`** — `longmemeval_adapter` does the same; `category_stats` now carries the three correctness numbers per question type alongside latency / belief counts. The multi-answer best-of wrapper handles LongMemEval's `answer: str | list[str]` shape. 6 unit tests.

## How it satisfies the acceptance criteria

| Criterion | Status |
|---|---|
| 1. `aelf bench all` returns non-trivial correctness for `amabench/_` and `longmemeval/_` | ✅ Three correctness leaves added per adapter; will populate next canonical capture |
| 2. Tolerance bands cover observed variance | ✅ Metric names ride the existing `tolerance.py` substring-match assignments (`exact_match` → ±10%, `f1` → ±7%); no `metric_overrides` needed because substring-EM and F1 are pure transforms — bit-deterministic across runs |
| 3. Bit-determinism contract holds | ✅ Scorers are pure stdlib transforms over `(prediction, ground_truth)` — no RNG, no time, no I/O. Verified by `test_determinism_repeated_calls` |
| 4. README badge can flip from "partial (6/11 adapters)" to "full (11/11 adapters)" | ✅ Both adapters now produce a deterministic correctness metric. Operator action: re-capture `benchmarks/results/v2.0.0.json` to fold the new leaves in, then flip the README badge |

## Why substring-EM is the canonical metric (not LLM-judge)

Issue body suggested either an LLM judge or "exact-match, F1, or substring-EM" — substring-EM is the deterministic option. There is no LLM prediction here: the adapter currently retrieves a context and exits. Substring-EM treats the retrieved context as the "prediction" and asks "did retrieval surface the gold answer span?" — that's the deterministic stand-in for downstream LLM correctness. Determinism preserves the bit-equality contract from acceptance #3.

An LLM-judge metric can still stack on top behind an opt-in flag (LongMemEval already has the `longmemeval_score.py` plumbing for that path), but it would break determinism and shouldn't be on the canonical cut.

## Out of scope

- Re-capturing `benchmarks/results/v2.0.0.json` with the new metrics (operator-side, separate run).
- Flipping the README badge from "partial (6/11)" to "full (11/11)" (depends on the recapture).
- StructMemEval composition zeros (#197 territory).
- Refactoring `mab_adapter.py` to use the new `qa_scoring` leaf — out of scope; MAB's local copy stays. Future cleanup can DRY them.

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest tests/test_bench_qa_scoring.py` — 24 / 24 pass
- [x] `pytest tests/test_amabench_scoring.py` — 6 / 6 pass
- [x] `pytest tests/test_longmemeval_scoring.py` — 6 / 6 pass
- [x] `pytest tests/test_bench_dispatcher.py tests/test_bench_tolerance.py tests/test_bench_qa_scoring.py tests/test_amabench_scoring.py tests/test_longmemeval_scoring.py` — 69 / 69 pass
- [x] `import benchmarks.amabench_adapter` and `import benchmarks.longmemeval_adapter` clean
- [x] Discretion grep on the diff returns no hits
- [x] All 3 commits signed (`%G?` = G)
- [ ] Operator: recapture `v2.0.0.json` after merge to populate new metric leaves and confirm tolerance bands hold across a 3-run calibration pass.

## Summary by Sourcery

Add deterministic QA correctness scoring to AMA-Bench and LongMemEval adapters using a shared stdlib-only scoring leaf, and expose aggregated correctness metrics alongside existing retrieval statistics.

New Features:
- Introduce a reusable qa_scoring module providing normalized exact match, substring exact match, F1, and multi-answer scoring helpers.
- Augment AMA-Bench adapter outputs with per-question and aggregated correctness metrics plus per-type and per-domain accuracy breakdowns.
- Augment LongMemEval adapter outputs with per-question and aggregated correctness metrics and include correctness stats in printed and JSON benchmark results.

Tests:
- Add unit tests for qa_scoring normalization, scoring functions, multi-answer logic, and determinism guarantees.
- Add AMA-Bench adapter tests covering score aggregation, legacy row handling, and per-type/domain accuracy helpers.
- Add LongMemEval adapter tests covering correctness aggregation, default values, and metric naming consistency with tolerance bands.

items.title: fix: calibrate profile-mismatch + risk scoring; correct dashboard & docs
items.body:
## What & why

Three calibration/accuracy fixes surfaced while preparing the Round-2 submission, validated on the IBM AML 100k benchmark. **44/44 tests pass.**

### 1. Profile-mismatch flood — `src/advanced_detectors.py`, `src/config_store.py`
The detector emitted an alert on a single weak behavioural rule *or* any edge with `ml_score ≥ 0.4`. On IBM AML (which carries no declared KYC profile) that produced **7,390 of 7,547 alerts** — 3,391 with zero behavioural mismatches, i.e. just re-labelling the ML classifier — so the Incidents view showed ~7,123 "incidents" (more than the analyst started with).

**Fix:** a Profile-Mismatch alert now requires the entity to violate its declared profile on **≥2 independent dimensions** (`profile_min_rule_score`, default 0.4, config-driven). The ML edge score still *escalates severity* for these corroborated cases but no longer manufactures an alert by itself (that signal already lives in edge scores / graph view / live scoring).
- Profile alerts **7,390 → 205**; total **7,547 → 562**; clustering becomes meaningful (**562 → 344** incidents).

### 2. Risk-weight LR quality gate — `src/run_pipeline.py`
The learned risk-weight LR was adopted unconditionally even at **F1 0.170 / AUC 0.705**, assigning ~0.45 risk to half the population → **36,274** nodes over 0.5. It silently overwrote the sensible hand-tuned scores.

**Fix:** adopt the learned weights only above a quality floor (`MIN_RW_F1 = 0.40`); otherwise keep the hand-tuned scores. High-risk entities **36,274 → 281** (now consistent with the detector summary).

### 3. Dashboard label — `frontend/src/pages/Dashboard.jsx`
The Fraud Volume card showed the *transaction-count* fraud rate (5.2%) labelled "of total", implying a volume percentage (₹18,707 cr is actually 31.8% of volume). Relabelled to "% of txns flagged".

### Docs — `README.md`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`
- README: removed 3 links to deleted `docs/*.tex` / `.mmd` files; corrected F1.
- ARCHITECTURE.md: endpoint count 30+ → 51; rewrote the stale synthetic-first cold start; split performance into per-txn (sub-ms) vs batch and fixed scale (~119k nodes / 87,772 edges); F1 → 0.617 / 0.927; clustering example updated to IBM AML reality.

## Verification
- **44/44 tests pass** after all changes.
- No code in `backend/` or `frontend/` depends on the removed `ml_only` / `scoring_mode` path.
- Risk-weight gate worst case = the original hand-tuned baseline, so it can't make scoring worse.
- Locked dashboard numbers, verified live: **100,000 txns · 562 alerts · 140 critical · 344 incidents · 281 high-risk · 562 open cases · F1 0.617 / AUC 0.927 · 310 velocity / 25 transit**.

## Note (intended behavioural change)
Profile-mismatch now requires ≥2 violations everywhere. The synthetic dataset embeds no profile-mismatch pattern, so it yields 0 profile alerts there by design — the other five detectors are unaffected (synthetic still produces 253 alerts), and the threshold is config-tunable.

items.title: Vault auto-unseal on Kubernetes restart and CI F1 validation gate
items.body:
## Summary

This PR addresses two reliability gaps in the platform: unattended Vault
sealing after Kubernetes restarts, and a broken CI quality gate that allowed
under-performing ML models to pass validation silently.

---

## Changes

### Vault Auto-Unseal on Kubernetes Restart

Previously, every Minikube restart left Vault sealed, requiring manual
`kubectl exec` intervention to unseal it. During that window, the backend
cannot connect to Vault, no credentials can be rotated, and the entire alert
pipeline goes dark.

**What was done:**
- Added an `unseal-watcher` sidecar container to the Vault StatefulSet. The
  sidecar polls Vault's seal status every 15 seconds and automatically calls
  `/v1/sys/unseal` whenever it detects a sealed state — no manual steps
  required after any restart.
- Added a dedicated `vault-sa` ServiceAccount and a least-privilege RBAC Role
  (`vault-rbac.yaml`) scoped to only what the Vault pod needs. The sidecar
  mounts the vault-data PVC as `readOnly: true` and carries no Vault token —
  it can trigger the unseal API but cannot read any secrets.
- Updated README and `docs/VAULT_GUIDE.md` to reflect the automated behaviour,
  including monitoring commands and the sidecar's security posture.

### CI F1 Validation Gate

The `Validate model performance` step in `ml-pipeline.yml` read the
`Best Threshold` line from `classification_report.txt` but never compared
anything against `MIN_F1_THRESHOLD`. A model with F1 = 0.01 would pass CI
and be uploaded as a release artifact.

**What was done:**
- Replaced the broken validation step with a real gate that parses the
  **Threat class F1 score** from the classification report using regex and
  calls `sys.exit(1)` if it falls below `MIN_F1_THRESHOLD` (default: 0.70).
  This blocks the artifact upload and fails the workflow on any under-performing
  model.
- Added a job summary step that writes a formatted results table (F1,
  precision, recall, best threshold, training duration) to
  `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`, visible directly in the PR UI.
- Added CI status badges to the README and a `Model Performance Gate` section
  documenting the threshold and how to adjust it.
- Added `backend/tests/test_ci_validation.py` with 6 unit tests covering the
  regex parsers, the pass/fail boundary, and malformed input handling.

---

## Testing

- CI pipeline (`ci.yml`) passes on all 6 checks — verified in commits
  `39073dd` and `ce00dcf`.
- Parser unit tests cover correct extraction, boundary conditions, and
  malformed report handling.
- Vault sidecar behaviour verified via `kubectl logs vault-0 -c unseal-watcher
  -n hpe` after a simulated restart.

---

## Files Changed

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `k8s/vault/vault-statefulset.yaml` | Added `unseal-watcher` sidecar |
| `k8s/vault/vault-rbac.yaml` | Added `vault-sa` ServiceAccount + Role |
| `.github/workflows/ml-pipeline.yml` | Real F1 gate + job summary step |
| `backend/tests/test_ci_validation.py` | Parser unit tests (new file) |
| `README.md` | CI badges, auto-unseal docs, Model Performance Gate section |
| `docs/VAULT_GUIDE.md` | Auto-Unseal, AppRole, Dynamic DB, Kafka creds sections |

items.title: analysis(z3): prove the emitted _fast adder's measurement-based uncompute (ADR 0027, F1/F2)
items.body:
Closes #67. Delivers the **optional stretch** of referee finding **F1/F2** (`paper/REVIEW.md`, ADR 0023): a z3/sim model of the HMR + `cz_if` phase correction the scored circuit actually runs. Complements the F1/F2 *disclosure* (ADR 0026, #57) — moves the MBUC phase correction from *disclosed-but-unproven* to **proven**.

## The gap (F1/F2)

The scored hot path emits `mod_add_qq_fast` / `mod_sub_qq_fast` / `mod_double_inplace_fast` — **58 fast calls vs 3 plain `mod_add_qq`** — all routing their addition through `cuccaro_add_fast` (`src/point_add/arith/adder.rs`). Its backward UMA sweep clears each carry ancilla with Gidney **measurement-based uncompute**: `b.hmr(carry, m)` (X-basis measure → outcome `m`, qubit reset, phase kickback `carry·m`) then `b.cz_if(x, y, m)` (conditional CZ applying `m·x·y`). Zero Toffoli — but correctness rests on those two phase terms **cancelling** (`carry·m ⊕ x·y·m = 0`) for *every* measurement outcome. The existing z3/Kani proofs model only the plain `mod_add_qq` and treat adders as exact integer `+`, so this phase-kickback logic had **zero symbolic coverage** — sampled-only.

## What's here

- **`src/point_add/mbuc_dump.rs`** (`#[cfg(test)]`) — dumps the **actually emitted** `cuccaro_add_fast` op-stream (widths 2..256, incl. production 256) from the real `B` builder to `analysis/mbuc_fast_adder_ops.json`. A non-ignored drift guard (`emitted_ops_match_committed_artifact`) fails loudly if the committed artifact ever diverges from a fresh emit — the proof verifies the **emitter's output, not a re-implementation** (the exact F2 concern).
- **`analysis/verify/mbuc_phase_correction.py`** — replays that op-stream through a z3 model of `src/sim.rs`'s per-op semantics (X/CX/CCX/CZ/Z/CCZ/HMR/R), with the measurement outcomes **free / universally quantified** (not the random XOF), proving per width:
  1. **functional** `acc' == (a + acc) mod 2^n`
  2. **clean** `a` unchanged, `c_in` + every carry back to `|0>`
  3. **phase-clean** net global phase `== 0` for **all** inputs and **all** measurement outcomes
  Teeth check: dropping the `cz_if` corrections makes claim (3) fail (z3 `sat`).
- `just mbuc` wired into the analysis chain (13→14 stages); **ADR 0027** + index; analysis README entry.

## Result

z3 discharges every width — including the production **256** — in ~2 s, all `unsat` on the negated claims, teeth firing at each width.

```
[PROVED] n=  2 … [PROVED] n=256: acc'=(a+acc) mod 2^n, a/c_in/carries clean,
                 phase=0 ∀ inputs ∧ ∀ outcomes; teeth: drop cz_if ⇒ phase≠0 [sat]
```

## Scope / isolation

Analysis layer only — a `verify/` z3 script + a `#[cfg(test)]` dump/guard; never compiled into `build_circuit`. Scored secp256k1 circuit **byte-identical** (`ops.bin` SHA `f30d8365c1235002`, rebuilt & verified). Proves the `cuccaro_add_fast` **primitive** (the shared MBUC carry-clear all `_fast` calls route through), not the whole composed 256-bit point-add — that remains the standing `scientific-value.md §4` stretch, stated honestly in ADR 0027.

Part of the referee-review remediation series (ADR 0023, #62). Uses ADR number **0027** to avoid collision with the parallel F3/F6-8/framing PRs (#64/#65 and the ADR 0026 cluster).

## Verification
- `just mbuc` — all widths PROVED incl. 256, teeth fire
- `cargo test --release --lib mbuc_dump` — drift guard passes
- `cargo fmt --check` clean; `python3 -m compileall` clean; `ops.bin` SHA unchanged

items.title: feat(bench): score a review against the answer key
items.body:
## Motivation

The bench could say a model made sixteen findings and anchored twelve of them where it quoted, for $1.22. It could not say whether any of the sixteen was one of the twenty things actually wrong with the change. Volume and price, measured carefully; correctness, not at all.

`bench/subjects/` has had the answer keys since #131 - twenty planted defects per pull request, each graded by how hard it was to find and keyed to a file and a line. Nothing read them. Scoring a review against one was a person with two documents open.

This is the measurement layer: precision, recall, recall per tier, and the discipline that makes those numbers worth reading.

## Implementation

**Findings arrive as data.** The harness asked for `--summary json` and nothing else, so all it knew about a review was one sentence. afi has written a findings document since `--review-json` existed, and it is the same list the sentence counts, so asking for it changes no number and is the difference between a finding that can be matched and one that can only be totted up. A caller may not redirect it: a second `--review-json` wins silently, and the run would be recorded, paid for, and scored as having found nothing.

**The keys are read, and checked.** They stay documents - the key is read by people far more often than by any parser, and an argument in a data format stops being read - but the headers already carry every field a matcher needs. What the checking catches is what no run would ever reveal: a defect graded tier 1 in the summary table and tier 2 in its own section, or keyed in a file the patch never touches. Either scores a real finding against the wrong tier or scores it as invented, and no number afterwards looks wrong. `mise run bench:keys` refuses both and runs in `check:bench`. The counts it reads back are the ones `bench/README.md` states by hand - 3/7/6/4 for the proxy, 3/4/6/8 for the dashboard, and so on - which is the closest thing to a proof the parser will get.

**Matching is locality, then a judge, and the two are kept apart.** Locality is arithmetic: same file, lines within three. It is wrong in one direction, and the proxy key shows how - one comment on `sweep.rs:102` is within three lines of three separate defects across three tiers, so arithmetic credits it with all three. So a record scored that way says `judged: false`, calls its recall an upper bound, and reports no precision at all: separating an invention from an intended trade-off needs someone to read the Not defects section.

**The judge is checked before it is believed.** It is asked one question - does this comment report this defect - and never whether a finding is useful, because the best published usefulness judge scores F1 0.76 at MCC -0.059. It must come from another model family, which `family.py` decides by reading afi's own table out of `src/config/review/family.rs` rather than keeping a copy that would drift silently in the flattering direction. Every verdict is cached in the run, so scoring stays free however often it runs. And `bench:judge -- kappa` measures it against a labelled set first; `bench:judge -- run` refuses any judge under 0.7. Kappa rather than agreement, because a judge answering "no" to everything agrees nine times in ten against a set that is ninety percent "no".

**What the labelled set is, and is not.** 135 pairs derived from the keys: 74 positives pairing a defect with a paraphrase of its own entry, and 61 negatives pairing that finding with a different defect locality cannot separate from it. The negatives are the hard half and the reason the set is worth having. It is *not* a hundred pairs hand-labelled from real reviews, which is what the issue asks for and what needs a filed pull request to exist; `bench/judge/README.md` says so plainly, and a kappa over this set is a floor rather than a licence.

**Configurations are named and fingerprinted.** `bench/variants.toml` holds five, and every run records the name plus a hash of what it resolved to - so two rows compare on the record rather than on a recollection. Keying on it fixed a real collapse: three variants of one model at one effort used to be one key, so a session measuring the default against two challengers reported the best of nine runs and discarded the comparison it existed to make. Trials needed no new spec field, only somewhere for the spread to go: p50, p95 and the findings range across a configuration's runs.

**The page shows all of it.** Two tables per subject rather than five more columns on one already twelve wide, six charts, the trials spread, and the grid that was actually missing - one row per keyed defect, one column per configuration, a tick or a dot. A recall of 55% says a model is middling; twenty rows say which nine it missed, and whether two models missed the same nine. The tier gradient is legible without reading a number. Drawing it means reading the keys for titles, so every record carries a fingerprint of the key it was scored against and a grid whose fingerprints have moved is withheld with a sentence rather than relabelling somebody's measurement. Everything the tables say on stderr, the page says on itself, now including what the judging cost.

**One thing this needed and did not have:** `--plan-only` on the runner. Every guard in it refuses a *shape*, and a plausible invocation passes all of them and goes straight to minting a provider key - so checking a spelling cost a provisioning call, and reading the output through a pipe that closed early cost a key that was minted and then not destroyed, because the cleanup trap is installed below the signal that killed it. It runs every check and stops at the last free line.

## What is not here

- **No measurement.** The registry is still empty and only cairn pull requests are measurable; none of the four subjects has been filed. Everything here was exercised with `--plan-only`, with fixtures, and with the judge's HTTP call stubbed. Nothing in this branch has spent money.
- **Clean diffs and noise-rate-on-clean**, the mutation-seeded stratum, `compare A B` with McNemar and the 6pp floor, and CI wiring - all still open on #96.
- **`afi review bench`** is still `mise run bench:*`. The harness mints and destroys provider keys, reads real bills, redacts and commits evidence, none of which belongs in the review binary; #97's own argument is that `afi review` should carry nothing it does not need per review.

## Checked

`mise run check` green. Both readers exercised against fixtures built to cover what real records cannot yet: four configurations over three variants, three trials each, one judged set and one not, a paid run nothing could score, a key edited after scoring. Every pure function carries doctests and `check:python` runs them; each new check was confirmed to fire by mutating a real key and a real reader and watching it fail. The judge's per-run accounting was verified with the call stubbed - six questions, $0.0060 asked for, $0.0060 the sum of what the records hold.

Follows #130, #131 and #132. Part of #97.
